Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 1:

(p-2) (Surat al-Anfal is Madani, and it has seventy-five verses.)

(In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.)

﴿They ask you about the spoils of war.﴾ Al-nafl (the spoils, booty) means ghanima (war booty). It was so named because it is a gift from Allah Most High, exceeding what is the basic reward for jihad in terms of the otherworldly recompense. The term is also applied to what is given by way of tanfil (extra bonus), in addition to one's share of the booty. It was also read as ʿalanfal, with the hamza dropped, its vowel transferred to the lam, and the nun of ʿan assimilated into the lam.

It is narrated that the Muslims disputed over the spoils of Badr and over their division. So they asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): How are they to be divided? And to whom does the ruling on them belong: to the Muhajirun, to the Ansar, or to all of them? It was also said that the young men had shown a fine performance on that day, killing seventy and taking seventy captives, so they said: "We are the fighters, and the spoils are ours." The elders and notables who were beside the banners said: "We were a reserve for you and a company to which you could retreat." Until Sa'd ibn Mu'adh said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "By Allah, what prevented us from seeking what these men sought was no indifference toward reward, nor cowardice before the enemy, but we disliked leaving your flank exposed, so that cavalry of the polytheists would attack you from the side." Then it was revealed.

It was also said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) had stipulated that whoever had a notable feat would be given a tanfil. That is why the young men did what they did of killing and capturing, and they asked him (ﷺ) for what he had stipulated for them. The elders said: The booty is small and the people are many, and if you give these men what you stipulated, you will deprive your companions." Then it was revealed.

The first view is the apparent one, since the question is a seeking of the ruling on the spoils, with the word ʿan governing it, not a request for the spoils themselves, as the last view states. The claim that ʿan is superfluous is manifest arbitrariness. Using as evidence the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, ʿAli ibn al-Husayn, Zayd, Muhammad al-Baqir, Ja'far al-Sadiq, ʿIkrima, and ʿAta, "yas'alunaka al-anfal" (they ask you the spoils), is not sound, for its basis, as they said, is elision and direct connection. This is indicated by the answer in His words, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Say: The spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger.﴾ That is, their ruling is exclusively His, Most High; the Messenger (ﷺ) divides them as he is commanded, without anyone's opinion entering into it. Had the question been a request for gifts, this would not be an answer to it, for the exclusivity of the ruling on what was stipulated for them to Allah and the Messenger does not contradict giving them to them; rather it realizes it, since they ask for them only by virtue of the Messenger's stipulation issued from him by the permission of Allah Most High, not by the ruling of having their hands reach them first. Interpreting the answer as meaning that the spoils, in the sense mentioned, belong exclusively to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), with no right in them for the one given the tanfil, whoever he may be, is certainly impossible, since the entitlement arises through tanfil. The claim that this entitlement was established by a later proof is an obligation of repeated abrogation without knowledge of the final abrogating text (p-3), and there is no justification for adopting the view of Mujahid, ʿIkrima and al-Suddi, that the spoils were exclusively for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so that no one had any share in them by this verse, and that it was then abrogated by His words, Most High: ﴿And know that whatever you gain of any thing, a fifth of it is for Allah and for the Messenger﴾. This is because, in their view, al-anfal necessarily means the first sense, as His words Most High indicate: ﴿And know that whatever you gain of any thing﴾ and so on.

Moreover, the truth is that there is no abrogation even then, as stated by ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam. Rather, at the beginning of the noble surah, it clarifies in summary that its matter is entrusted to Allah Most High and His Messenger, and then it explains its expenditures and the manner of their division in detail. The claim that this ruling, namely exclusivity to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), is restricted to the spoils stipulated on the day of Badr, making the lam one of specific reference, while the entitlement of the one given tanfil remains in the other stipulated spoils, is rejected by the context of stating rulings, as indicated by the placing of "al-anfal" in the position where a pronoun would be expected. Furthermore, answering a question about gifts promised by stating that they belong to him (ﷺ) exclusively is not fitting to his noble station at all. It has been narrated from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas that he said: "My brother ʿUmayr was killed on the day of Badr, so I killed Sa'id ibn al-As in revenge for him, and I took his sword, which pleased me. I brought it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: Allah Most High has healed my chest from the polytheists, so give me this sword. He (ﷺ) said to me: This is neither mine nor yours; throw it into the pile. So I threw it, and I had within me what none knows but Allah, of the killing of my brother and the taking of his spoils. I had not gone far when Surat al-Anfal was revealed, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: O Sa'd, you asked me for the sword when it was not mine, but now it has become mine, so go and take it."

This, as you see, requires that the tanfil had not taken place on that day, for otherwise Sa'd's request for the sword would have been by virtue of his stipulation and promise (ﷺ), not as an unprompted gift. Attributing that to Sa'd's observance of courtesy does not work, since his request was by virtue of the stipulation, and the Messenger's refusal before the revelation refutes it. His explanation, "This is not mine," is the impossibility that he would promise what he could not fulfill. His giving after the revelation, and his ordering it upon the words "it has now become mine," is because the basis of its becoming his (ﷺ) is the words of Allah Most High: ﴿The spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger﴾, and the assumption is that this was what prevented giving what was asked. Among the texts decisive on this matter is the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿So fear Allah﴾, that is, since the matter of the spoils belongs to Allah Most High and His Messenger, fear Him, and avoid what you were engaged in of quarreling over them and disputing that brings the wrath of Allah Most High. Or it means: fear Him in all that you do and all that you leave undone, so that what they were in enters primarily into it.

Had the question been a request for what was stipulated, there would be no prohibition in it requiring avoidance. The mention of the glorious Name serves to cultivate awe and to give the reason for the ruling.

﴿And set right what is between you﴾ The state that obtains among them is treated as a companion to their complete involvement with it, just as the hidden matters in the breasts are called "possessors of the breasts." That is: set right your mutual situations by mutual consolation and assistance in what Allah Most High has provided and bestowed upon you. ʿUbada ibn al-Samit reported: It was revealed concerning us, the company of Badr, when we disputed over the nafl and our tempers were ruffled over it, so Allah Most High took it from our hands and made it for His Messenger, who divided it among the Muslims equally. In that there was taqwa of Allah, obedience to His Messenger, and setting right of what is between people.

ʿAta reported: The setting right among them was that he called them and said: Divide your spoils with justice. They said: We have eaten and spent. He said: Then let some of you return to others.

﴿And obey Allah and His Messenger﴾ by submitting to his command and prohibition. The placing of the command to set right what is between people between the command to taqwa and the command to obey serves to show the full care for reconciliation as the situation requires, and so that the command to it falls under the command to obey. ﴿If you are believers﴾ is connected to the three commands, and the answer is omitted, relying on what has been mentioned as indicating it; or it is the answer according to the well-known difference of opinion. In either case, the aim is to affirm the conditional on the basis of the realization of what it is conditioned upon. This contains encouragement for the addressees and urges them to hasten to comply (p-4). By faith is meant its perfection, that is: if you are of perfect faith, for perfection of faith turns on these three qualities: obeying commands, avoiding sins, and setting right what is between people with justice and kindness.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 2:

﴿Indeed, the believers﴾ is a resumptive sentence (jumlah musta'nafah), brought to explain who is meant by "the believers," by mentioning their sublime attributes, which entail the three qualities mentioned, and in it there is additional encouragement for them to comply with the commands mentioned; that is: indeed, those who are perfect in faith and sincere in it are ﴿those whose hearts tremble when God is mentioned﴾. That is: they are struck with fear merely by the mention of Him, without there being mentioned there anything that necessitates fear of His attributes and actions, out of magnifying His sublime station and being in awe of Him. It has also been said: this refers to the man who intends an act of disobedience, and it is said to him, "Fear God," so he refrains from it out of fear of His punishment. It was also read as (wajilat) with a fatha on the jim, which is a dialect form, and it was read as (fariqat), meaning: feared.

﴿And when His verses are recited to them﴾, whatever verse it may be, ﴿they increase them in faith﴾, that is: in certainty and tranquility of soul, for the convergence of proofs and the mutual support of arguments and demonstrations necessitates an increase in assurance and strength of certainty. It has also been said that faith itself does not admit of increase and decrease; rather its increase is by reason of the increase in what is believed, for whenever a verse is revealed and the believer affirms it, his faith increases in number. As for faith itself, it remains in its state. It has also been said: it is by reason of the fact that deeds are counted as part of faith, so it increases with their increase. The more correct view is that assent itself admits of strength, and this is what is expressed by "increase," for the clear distinction between the certainty of the prophets and of those who attain unveiling (ahl al-mukashafat) and the certainty of ordinary members of the community. On this is based the saying of 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: "Had the veil been lifted, I would not have increased in certainty." Likewise, there is a difference between what is established by a single proof and what is established by many proofs.

﴿And upon their Lord﴾, their Owner and the Manager of their affairs exclusively, ﴿they rely﴾, that is: they entrust their affairs to no one other than Him. The clause is coordinated with the relative clause (al-silah), and His saying, exalted is He:

﴿Those who establish the prayer and spend out of what We have provided for them﴾ is in the nominative case, either as a qualifier (*na't*, an adjective modifying) of the first relative pronoun (*al-mawsul al-awwal*), or as an apposition (*badal*, a substitute) for it, or as an explanatory apposition (*bayan*) for it. Alternatively, it is in the accusative case by way of *qat'* (grammatical separation from the preceding noun), which indicates praise. He first mentioned among their good deeds the deeds of the heart: fear (*khashyah*), sincerity (*ikhlas*), and reliance on God (*tawakkul*). Then he followed them with the deeds of the limbs: the prayer (*salah*) and charity (*sadaqah*).

This is the commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 4:

﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to those whose praiseworthy attributes were mentioned, in that they are characterized by them. It indicates that they are distinguished by this from all others in the most complete distinction, and that by means of it they are placed within the row of visible matters. The sense of distance in it serves to announce the elevation of their rank and the remoteness of their station in nobility. ﴿They are the believers truly.﴾ This is because they realized their faith by joining to it the excellent deeds, both of the heart and of the body, that were detailed.

"Ḥaqqan" (حَقًّا, "truly") is an adjective modifying a omitted verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: "Those are the believers with a true faith." Or it is a verbal noun emphasizing the sentence, meaning: "That has been truly established," like your saying: "He is truly the servant of God."

﴿For them are degrees﴾ of honor and nearness [to God]. It has been said: they are high degrees in Paradise. This may be either a new independent sentence (mubtada', a "subject-initiated" sentence), built upon a question arising from the enumeration of their virtues, as if it were said: "What is theirs in return for these qualities?" So it is said: "For them is such-and-such." Or it is a second predicate (khabar thani) for "those." The words of Him, exalted is He, ﴿with their Lord﴾ are either connected to an omitted element that occurs as a descriptive modifier of "degrees" to emphasize it, since the nunation (tanwin) conveys inherent grandeur, reinforced by the grandeur of the annexed form, meaning: "existing with Him, exalted is He." Or they are connected to what the predicate depends on, namely the sense of "stability" that belongs to them. The annexing of the adverbial phrase to "Lord," itself annexed to their pronoun, conveys added honor and kindness to them, and announces that what was promised them is absolutely certain in its occurrence and attainment, secure from being lost.

﴿And forgiveness﴾ for what they committed of shortcomings, ﴿and a generous provision﴾ that its duration does not end and its number does not run out, which is what has been prepared for them of the bliss of Paradise.

﴿As your Lord brought you out of your house in truth﴾. The *kaf* (the particle "like") is in the place of nominative case (*mahal al-raf'*, the grammatical position that would take a nominative ending), as the predicate (*khabar*, the predicate of a nominal sentence) of an omitted subject (*mubtada'*, the topic of a nominal sentence). Its estimate is: "This state is like the state of your bringing forth", meaning: their state in disliking what you saw, though it is true, is like their state in disliking your going out to war, which is also true. Or it is in the place of accusative case, as a qualifier (*sifah*, an adjectival modifier) of an omitted verbal noun (*masdar*, the verbal noun) in His saying, ﴿The spoils belong to Allah﴾, meaning: the spoils were established for Allah and the Messenger despite their dislike, with an establishment like the establishment of your Lord's bringing you out of your house in Madinah, or from Madinah, a bringing out connected with truth.

﴿And indeed, a group of the believers were averse﴾. That is: while a group of them were averse to going out, either due to the natural disinclination of the soul toward fighting, or due to lack of readiness. This was because the caravan of Quraysh came from Syria, carrying great trade, and with it forty riders, among them Abu Sufyan, 'Amr ibn al-'As, and 'Amr ibn Hisham. Jibril informed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he informed the Muslims. They were pleased to intercept the caravan because of its abundant wealth and the smallness of the people (escorting it). When they set out, the news reached the people of Makkah of their departure. Abu Jahl called out from atop the Ka'bah to the people of Makkah: "Rescue! Rescue! Upon every mount, swift or slow, your caravan, your wealth! If Muhammad seizes it, you will never prosper after it, ever."

The sister of al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib (may Allah be pleased with him) saw a dream and told her brother: "I saw as if a angel descended from the sky, took a rock from the mountain, then flew with it, and there was not a house in Makkah but that a stone from that rock struck it." Al-'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated it, and Abu Jahl said: "Our men are not content to prophesy until our women prophesy!" Abu Jahl set out with all the people of Makkah, and they were the *nafir* (the mobilized war host). It was said to him: "The caravan has taken the coastal road and escaped, so turn back with the people to Makkah." He said: "No, by al-Lat, that will never happen until we slaughter camels, drink wine, and have singing girls and musical instruments at Badr, so that all the Arabs hear of our departure and that Muhammad did not seize the caravan, and that we have stung him." So he proceeded with them to Badr. Badr is a water-place where the Arabs used to gather for their market one day in the year. Then Jibril (peace be upon him) descended and said: "O Muhammad, indeed Allah promised you one of the two groups, either the caravan or Quraysh." The Prophet (ﷺ) consulted his companions and said: "What do you say? The people have set out from Makkah upon every mount, swift or slow. Is the caravan dearer to you, or the war host?" They said: "Rather, the caravan is dearer to us than meeting the enemy." The face of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) changed, then he repeated to them and said: "Indeed the caravan has passed along the seashore, and here is Abu Jahl approaching." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, take the caravan and leave the enemy." Then, when the Prophet (ﷺ) was angered, Abu Bakr and 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with both of them) rose and spoke well. Then Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah rose and said: "Look to your affair and proceed. By Allah, if you were to travel to 'Adan Abyan, no man of the Ansar would stay behind you." Then al-Miqdad ibn 'Amr (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "O Messenger of Allah, proceed with what Allah has commanded you, for we are with you wherever you wish. We will not say to you as the Children of Israel said to Musa (peace be upon him): 'Go, you and your Lord, and fight; indeed we are sitting here.' Rather: 'Go, you and your Lord, and fight; indeed we are fighting along with you.'" (p-6) "As long as one of our eyes blinks." The Prophet (ﷺ) laughed, then said: "Advise me, O people," meaning the Ansar, because they had said to him when they pledged allegiance to him at the 'Aqabah: "We are free of your protection until you reach our homes. When you reach us, you are under our protection; we will protect you as we protect our sons and wives." The Prophet (ﷺ) feared that the Ansar would not consider their support of him obligatory except against an enemy who attacked them in Madinah. Then Sa'd ibn Mu'adh rose and said: "It seems you mean us, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "Yes." He said: "We have believed in you and affirmed you, and we testified that what you brought is the truth, and we gave you on that our covenants and pledges of hearing and obedience. So proceed, O Messenger of Allah, with what you intend. By Him who sent you with truth, if you were to lead us into this sea and plunge into it, we would plunge with you; not one man of us would stay behind. We do not dislike that you meet our enemy with us. We are steadfast in war and truthful at encounter. Perhaps Allah will show you from us what will delight your eye. So march with us in the blessing of Allah." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rejoiced, and the words of Sa'd gladdened him. Then he said: "Proceed in the blessing of Allah and rejoice, for Allah has promised me one of the two groups. By Allah, as if I now see the places where the people will fall."

It is narrated that it was said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he finished with Badr: "Pursue the caravan, nothing stands between you and it." Al-'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him), who was in his bonds, called out to him: "It is not right." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Why?" He said: "Because Allah promised you one of the two groups, and He has given you what He promised you."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 6:

﴿They dispute with you concerning the truth﴾ — namely, the encounter with the armed host (nafir) — because they preferred it to the encounter with the caravan (ir). The clause is either a resumed statement (isti'naf) or a second circumstantial clause (hal thaniya), i.e., "He brought you forth while they were disputing with you." It may also be a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the pronoun in ﴿lakarihun﴾ (certainly averse). The phrase ﴿after it had become clear﴾ is in the accusative governed by ﴿yujadilunaka﴾ (they dispute with you), and "ma" is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyya), meaning: after the truth had become clear to them through your informing them that they would be given victory wherever they turned. They would say, "We did not set out except for the caravan; why did you not tell us so that we might prepare and get ready?" This was on account of their aversion to fighting.

﴿As though they were being driven to death﴾ — the kaf (ka) is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the pronoun in ﴿lakarihun﴾, meaning: likened to those who are driven with violence and humiliation to be killed. ﴿While they are looking on﴾ is a circumstantial clause referring to the pronoun in ﴿yusaquna﴾ (they are driven), meaning: and the state is that they are looking at the causes of death and witnessing them with their own eyes. This degree of fear and dismay was only due to the smallness of their number, their lack of preparation, and their being foot soldiers. It is narrated that there were only two horsemen among them.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 8, verse 7:**

﴿And when Allah promised you one of the two groups﴾ is a resumptive statement (*kalam mustaʾnaf*), brought in to show the beautiful way in which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, dealt with the believers, despite their lack of resolve (*qillat al-hazm*), their meanness of aspiration (*danaʾat al-himma*), their shallowness of judgment (*qusur al-ra'y*), and their fear and anxiety. The word "*idh*" (إذْ) is in the accusative as an object, governed by an implied verb addressed to the believers through a shift and variation of address (*al-talwin wal-iltifat*, the change of grammatical person within discourse). "*Iḥdā al-ṭāʾifatayn*" (إحْدى الطّائِفَتَيْنِ) is the second object of "*yaʿidukum*." The meaning is: remember the time when Allah promised you one of the two groups.

Mentioning "the time" (*al-waqt*) when the intended meaning is the events that occurred in it is a way of emphasizing, as has been noted many times before, the importance of remembering them. Commanding remembrance of the time is, by demonstrative reasoning, a command to remember what happened in it. Moreover, the time encompasses the events that took place in it with all their details, so when it is recalled, what happened in it is present in detail, as if it were witnessed directly.

It is read "*yaʿidkum*" (يَعِدْكُمْ) with the *dal* sukun for lightness. The imperfect form is used to narrate a past situation in the present, to bring its image vividly to mind. The words of the Most High, "*annahā lakum*" (أنَّها لَكُمْ), are a substitution of inclusion (*badal ishtimal*, a substitute that is related to the thing it replaces by way of association) for "*iḥdā al-ṭāʾifatayn*," explaining the manner of the promise. That is: He promises you that one of the two groups is for you, specifically yours, subjected to you, and you will exercise authority over it as owners do, and you will dispose of them as you wish.

﴿And you wished﴾ is coordinated with "*yaʿidukum*" and falls under the command to remember. That is: you loved (*tuhibbūna*) that ﴿the one without the thorn of battle be yours﴾ from the two groups, rather than the one with the thorn, which was the army (*al-nafīr*), whose leader was Abu Jahl and who numbered a thousand fighters. "The one without the thorn" (*ghayr dhāt al-shawka*) was the caravan (*al-ʿīr*), in which there were only forty horsemen, whose leader was Abu Sufyan. The description of them by this title alerts to the reason for their desire to encounter it and the cause of their aversion and reluctance to meet the army. "*Al-shawka*" means sharpness (*al-ḥidda*), used metaphorically from the single thorn (*wāḥidat al-shawk*), and "*shawk al-qanā*" means the point of the spear.

﴿And Allah wished﴾ is coordinated with "*tawaddūna*" and is included with it in the sequence of remembrance, to show them the great kindness of Allah toward them despite the meanness of their aspirations and the shallowness of their judgment. That is: remember the time of His, the Most High's, promise to you of one of the two groups, and your love for the lesser of them, and His, the Most High's, will for the greater of them. This is expressed in His words: ﴿to establish the truth﴾, that is, to confirm it and make it prevail, ﴿by His words﴾, that is, by His revelations sent down concerning this matter, or by His commands to the angels to provide reinforcement, and by what He decreed of their capture, killing, and throwing into the well of Badr. It is also read "*bi-kalimatihi*" (بِكَلِمَتِهِ) in the singular.

﴿and to cut off the root of the disbelievers﴾, that is, their last remnant, and to uproot them completely. The meaning is: you desire the trivial matters, while Allah, Mighty and Exalted, desires their lofty ones, and what returns to the elevation of the Word of Truth and the sublimity of the rank of the religion. How far apart are the two desires! And the words of the Most High:

This is the commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 8:

﴿That He may establish the truth and nullify falsehood﴾ is a resumptive (new) sentence (jumla mustaʾnafa), brought to explain the wisdom (hikma) that prompted the choice of the one with the power (dhat al-shawka), and their victory over it, despite their desire for the other. The lam (of purpose) is connected to a suppressed verb (fiʿl muqaddar) placed after it, i.e., "for this sublime end He did what He did and for nothing else." There is no repetition in this, since the first (statement) explains the disparity between the two desires, while this one explains the wisdom that prompted what was mentioned. The meaning of "establishing the truth" (ihqaq al-haqq) is the manifestation of its truthfulness, not making it true after it was not so; and likewise the case of "nullifying falsehood" (ibtal al-batil). ﴿And though the criminals dislike it﴾, i.e., the polytheists (al-mushrikin) dislike that, namely the establishing of the truth and the nullifying of falsehood.

﴿When you were calling upon your Lord for help﴾ is a *badal* (substitute, or apposition) for ﴿when He promised you﴾ and is governed by the same governing verb (*ʿamil*). The meaning is to remind them of their seeking help from Him, glorified is He, and their turning to Him, exalted is He, when their means were exhausted and their excuses failed them, and of His provision of help to them at that time. It has also been said that it is connected to His words, exalted is He, ﴿that He might establish the truth﴾, as an adverbial of time (*ẓarfiyyah*). As for what has been said, that His words ﴿that He might establish﴾ are in the future tense, because it is governed by *an* (the particle that puts the verb in the subjunctive), and so it cannot govern ﴿idh﴾ (when), since ﴿idh﴾ is an adverb of past time, this is not correct. This is because its being future is only in relation to the time of the thing for which it is the goal from the implied verb, not in relation to the time of the seeking of help, so that it would not govern it. Rather, both occurred at one time. The time of the seeking of help was expressed by ﴿idh﴾ only with regard to the time of the descent (of the angels). The future form in ﴿you are calling﴾ is to narrate the past situation, to bring its wondrous image to mind. It has also been said that it is connected to an implied, new (independent) verb, meaning: remember the time of your seeking help. That is because when they knew that fighting was unavoidable, they began to call upon Allah, exalted is He, saying: "O Lord, help us against Your enemy; O Helper of those who seek help, aid us."

It is related from ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, that: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) looked at the polytheists, who were a thousand, and at his companions, who were three hundred and some ten, so he faced the qiblah, stretched out his hands, and supplicated: (p-8) 'O Allah, fulfil for me what You have promised me. O Allah, if this small band perishes, You will not be worshipped on the earth.' He continued in this state until his cloak fell from his shoulders. Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, picked it up, placed it on his shoulder, embraced him from behind, and said: 'O Prophet of Allah, your insistent pleading with your Lord is enough, for He will surely fulfil for you what He has promised you.'"

﴿So He answered you﴾ is conjoined (*ʿatf*) to ﴿you were calling﴾ and is included with it in the sense of reminder, as you know it is in the past tense. The future form is to bring the scene to mind. ﴿That I am sending you reinforcements﴾: that is, ﴿bi-anni﴾ (with the fact that I), so the preposition was deleted and the verb was made to govern it, so its position became accusative. It was also read with a kasra on the hamzah, either to mean the sense of saying, or by treating ﴿istajaba﴾ (answered) as ﴿qāla﴾ (said), because answering is among the things that are said. ﴿With a thousand of the angels, following one another﴾: that is, making others of the angels follow after themselves. So what is meant by them are their chiefs, who bring others after them. Here He has been content with this general statement, and in Sūrat Āl ʿImrān He clarified the number of them. It has also been said that the meaning is: following themselves with other angels, or following the believers, or following one another, from *ardaftuhu* (I made him follow), when you come after him; or following the believers themselves, from *ardaftuhu iyyāhu* (I made him follow me) so he followed.

It is also read *murdafīn* with a fatḥah on the *dāl*, meaning: followed, or being followed, in the sense that they were the vanguard of the army or its rear guard. It is also read *murridfīn* with a kasrah or a ḍammah on the *rāʾ* and a shaddah on the *dāl*. Its original form is *murtadifīn* (in the sense of coming one after another), so the *tāʾ* was assimilated into the *dāl*, the two consonants met, so the *rāʾ* was given a kasrah according to the original form, or a ḍammah by way of assimilation to the following sound. It is also read *bi-ālāf* (with thousands) to agree with what is in Sūrat Āl ʿImrān. The way of reconciling this with the well-known reading is that what is meant by "a thousand" are those who were at the vanguard, or the rear guard, or their notables and leaders, or those among them who fought. There is disagreement over whether they fought, and reports have been narrated that indicate that it occurred.

[And Allah did not make it] is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*), brought in to show that apparent causes have no real effect of their own. Effect belongs to Him alone, Exalted and Majestic, so that the believers might put their trust in Him and not despair of victory when its causes are lacking. The verb *ja'l* (making, appointing) is transitive to one object, which is the pronoun referring back to the verbal noun of an implied verb that the context strongly requires, so that it need not be stated. It is as if it were said: "So We will reinforce you with them, and Allah did not make your reinforcement with them [anything] except as glad tidings." The phrase ﴿except as glad tidings﴾ is an exceptive construction with an omitted antecedent (*istithna' mufarragh*) drawn from the most general category of causes (*a'amm al-'ilal*). That is: Allah did not make your reinforcement through the sending down of the angels, visibly, for anything except as glad tidings to you that you would be given victory. ﴿And that your hearts might be at rest thereby﴾ means: by the reinforcement, and that your souls might find tranquility in it, just as tranquility was for the Children of Israel in the same way. Both ﴿glad tidings﴾ and ﴿that your hearts might be at rest﴾ are objects of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*) for the verb *ja'l*. The first has been put in the accusative because its conditions were met, while the second remained in its original form because those conditions were absent. It has also been said that this is to indicate that the second is primary in causation and significant in itself, as was said regarding the words of the Exalted: ﴿And the horses, mules and donkeys, for you to ride and as adornment﴾. Restricting the reinforcement to these two (glad tidings and tranquility) indicates that the angels do not directly take part in fighting. Their reinforcement was rather by strengthening the hearts of those who fight and increasing their numbers and the like, as is the view of some of the early generations (*al-salaf*).

It has also been said that the verb *ja'l* is transitive to two objects, the second being ﴿except as glad tidings﴾, on the basis that it is an exception from the most general of the objects. That is: Allah did not make it anything among things except as good news for you. In that case, the *lam* in ﴿and that your hearts might be at rest﴾ is connected to an omitted element placed later, its estimated form being: "and that your hearts might be at rest thereby, He did this and not for anything else."

﴿And victory is not⦅ ⦆ [the reality of victory in the absolute sense]﴾, meaning the true reality of victory without qualification, ﴿except from Allah﴾, meaning it is only something that comes from Him, Exalted and Majestic, without there being any partnership in it on the part of causes or numbers. Rather, these are merely manifestations of Him, by way of the continuing course of the divine custom (*sunnah*).

﴿Indeed Allah is Mighty﴾, not overcome in His judgment and not disputed in His decrees, ﴿Wise﴾, doing everything He does as wisdom and benefit require. The sentence serves as a reason for what precedes it, containing an implication that victory occurring in the manner mentioned is one of the requirements of far-reaching wisdoms.

[p-9]

﴿When He covers you with drowsiness﴾, i.e., He makes it envelop you and surround you. It is a second substitute (*badal*, apposition) for "when He promised you," to show another favour. The imperfect form used here and in what is conjoined to it is for narrating a past situation, as in (تَسْتَغِيثُونَ). Alternatively, it is governed by an implied "remember" (اذْكُرُوا). It was also said that it is connected to "victory," or to what is in "from the presence of Allah" of the sense of a verb, or to "making." But this is not clear. It is read as (يُغْشِيكُمُ), from *ighsha'* (causing to cover), in the sense of *taghshiya* (covering), and the agent in both cases is the Creator, exalted is He. It is also read as (يَغْشاكُمُ), with the verb attributed to drowsiness. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿as a security from Him﴾, in the first two readings, is in the accusative of purpose (*al-'illiyya*), governed by a verb that follows from the mentioned verb: that is, "He covers you with drowsiness, so you doze off as a security that is from Allah, exalted is He, not as exhaustion and weariness." Or it is a verbal noun (*masdar*) of another verb of the same kind, meaning "so you feel secure, a security," as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and caused it to grow a good growth﴾, according to one of the two views. It was also said that it is in the accusative governed by the mentioned verb itself, and that *al-amana* has the meaning of *al-iman* (faith). In the last reading, it is in the accusative of purpose governed by (يَغْشاكم) according to meaning, since it has the force of "you doze off." Or it is a verbal noun of a verb that follows from it, as has passed. It is also read as (أمْنَةً), like (رَحْمَةٍ). ﴿And sends down upon you water from the sky﴾. The fronting of the prepositional phrase before the object is for the reason already mentioned many times: attention to what is fronted and creating anticipation for what is delayed. When what should be fronted is delayed, the soul remains waiting for it, and upon its arrival it settles in with especially firm settlement. The fronting of (عَلَيْكُمْ) is because showing that the sending down is upon them is more important than showing that it is from the sky. It is also read with the lightened form, from *inzal* (sending down). ﴿To purify you by it﴾, i.e., from the minor and major ritual impurity (*hadath asghar wa akbar*). ﴿And to remove from you the defilement of Satan﴾. The discussion of the fronting of the prepositional phrase is as has passed just now. What is meant by "the defilement of Satan" is his whispering and his frightening them with thirst.

It is related that they alighted in a reddish sand dune in which feet sink, without water, and they slept, and most of them had wet dreams. The polytheists had overpowered them at the water. Satan appeared to them and whispered to them, saying: "You, companions of Muhammad, claim that you are upon the truth, and that you pray without ablution and in a state of major impurity, and you are thirsty. If you were upon the truth, these people would not have overpowered you at the water. They are only waiting for thirst to exhaust you, and when it cuts your necks, they will come to you, kill whomever they love, and drive the rest of you to Makkah." So they grieved a severe grief and became apprehensive. Then Allah, mighty and majestic is He, sent down rain, and they were rained upon at night until the valley flowed. They washed and performed ablution, watered the mounts, and the sand that had been between them and the enemy became packed down, so that feet were firm upon it. The whispering of Satan went away, souls were content, and hearts were strengthened. This is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and to strengthen your hearts﴾, i.e., to make them strong with confidence in the subtle kindness of Allah, exalted is He, after witnessing its first signs, ﴿and make your feet firm thereby﴾, so that they do not sink into the sand. Thus the pronoun refers to the water, as in the first instance. It is also permissible that it refers to the strengthening, for when the heart becomes strong and patience and boldness settle in it, the foot hardly slips in the battlefields of war. And His saying, exalted is He,(p-10)

"When your Lord revealed to the angels": (إذْ يُوحِي رَبُّكَ إلى المَلائِكَةِ) is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb that begins a new sentence (mudmar mustaʾnaf). It is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ in the mode of abstraction (tajrid), as indicated by the kaf (the second-person pronoun), because the matter commanded is one that no one other than him ﷺ could undertake. For the revelation mentioned here, before it became manifest through the recited revelation upon his tongue ﷺ, is not among the blessings on which the general community stands, like the other earlier blessings which they were commanded to mention at their time by way of thankfulness.

It has been said: it is in the accusative governed by His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿and He might fortify thereby your feet﴾. In that case, the pronoun in bihi (thereby) must refer to "the binding upon the hearts" (al-rabt ʿala al-qulub), so that the meaning becomes: "and He might fortify your feet by strengthening your hearts at the time of His revealing to the angels and His commanding them to make you firm, which is the time of fighting." It is not hidden that restricting the said firming to an indefinite time, in their estimation, adds no extra benefit. As for its being in the accusative as a third substitute (badal) for (idh yaʿiduka-kum) ["when He promised you"], as has been said, this is rejected by the specification of the address to him ﷺ, together with what you have learned: that the matter commanded is not among the general duties common to all, like its sister [matters].

Mentioning the title of Lordship (al-rububiyya) with its attachment to his ﷺ pronoun contains an honouring and an exaltation that are not hidden.

The meaning is: "Remember the time of His, the Exalted's, revealing to the angels ﴿that I am with you﴾," that is, by reinforcement and enabling in the matter of firming. Thus it is the object of "He reveals" (yuhi). It is read with kasra [i.e., innī] in view of intending speech, or treating revelation as having its status. What the presence of the word "with" (maʿa) suggests of the angels being followers is only from the standpoint that they are the ones directly carrying out the firming in outward form; so they have precedence from that standpoint, as in such sayings of His, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, God is with the patient﴾. The fa' in His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿so firm up those who have believed﴾ is for the sequencing of what follows upon what precedes, for His support of them is among the strongest reasons for firming.

They differed regarding the manner of the firming. A group said: they were only commanded to firm them by good tidings, increasing their numbers, and similar things by which their hearts are strengthened, their resolutions and intentions become sound, and their zeal in fighting is reinforced. This is the most fitting to the meaning of firming and its reality, which is an expression for urging toward steadfastness in the place of swords and exertion in bearing the hardships of fighting.

It has been narrated that the angel would take the form of a man whom they recognized by face; he would come and say: "I heard the polytheists saying: 'By God, if they charge upon us, we will surely be routed,'" and he would walk between the two rows saying: "Rejoice, for God, the Exalted, is your helper." Others said: they were commanded to fight their enemies, and they made His, the Exalted's, words ﴿I shall cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved﴾ an explanation of His words ﴿that I am with you﴾, and His words ﴿so strike﴾ ... etc. an explanation of His words ﴿so firm up﴾, clarifying the manner of the firming.

It has been narrated from Abu Dawud al-Mazini, may God be pleased with him, and he was among those who witnessed Badr, that he said: "I pursued a man from the polytheists on the day of Badr in order to strike him, and his head fell before my sword reached him." And from Sahl ibn Hunayf, may God be pleased with him, that he said: "We saw ourselves on the day of Badr, and one of us would point his sword at a polytheist, and his head would fall from his body before the sword reached him."

You know well that their killing of the disbelievers, although it does not suit the meaning of firming the believers, is not something that depends on the assistance by casting terror; so the ordering of the command upon it with the fa' is not appropriate. The earlier scholars have excused this by saying that His words ﴿I shall cast...﴾ ... etc. are not explicit regarding what was mentioned; rather it is possible that this came right after His words ﴿so firm up those who have believed﴾, as instruction to the angels of what they might firm them with, as if it were said: "Say to them: ﴿I shall cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved, so strike⦆ ... etc."

So the strikers are the believers. As for what has been said, that this is a direct address from Him, the Exalted, to the believers by way of a shift of address (talwin), its basis is a supposition that it came before the fighting; but how could that be? The noble surah was revealed only after the battle had been completed. His words ﴿above the necks﴾ mean: their high parts, which are the places of slaughter or the heads ﴿and strike from them every fingertip﴾. It has been said: al-banan are the tips of the fingers of the hands and feet. It has been said: they are the fingers of the hands and feet. Abu al-Haytham said: al-banan are the joints, and every joint is a banana. Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Jurayj and al-Dahhak said: it means the extremities, that is: strike them in all the limbs, from their upper parts to their lower parts. It has been said: the intended meaning of al-banan is the lower parts, and of "above the necks" the upper parts, and the meaning is: strike the leaders and the lowly. The repetition of the command to strike is for added emphasis and concern with its matter. And "from them" is connected to it, or to an omitted element that falls as a circumstantial phrase (hal) relating to what follows.

"Dhalika" (that) is a reference to the punishment that befell them, and the demonstrative with the sense of distance in it serves to indicate how far its degree is in severity and dreadfulness. The address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), or to everyone who is fit to be addressed. Its position is in the nominative, as the subject of a nominal sentence, and its predicate is the words of the Exalted: ﴿because they opposed God and His Messenger﴾. That is: this dreadful punishment befalls them on account of their opposing and contending against One against whom there is no way at all to contend. The derivation of "mushaqqa" (opposition) is from "shiqq" (side), because each of the two opponents is on a side different from the side of the other, just as the derivation of "mu'adah" (enmity) and "mukhasama" (contention) is from "'adwa" and "khasm," meaning the side, because each of the two enemies and the two disputants is on an 'adwa and a khasm different from the 'adwa and khasm of the other.

﴿And whoever opposes God and His Messenger﴾: the explicit mention in place of the pronoun serves to cultivate awe, to show the full enormity of what they dared to do, and to signal the reason for the ruling. And the words of the Exalted: ﴿then indeed God is severe in punishment﴾ are either the apodosis itself, from which the returning pronoun referring to "man" has been deleted according to those who require it, meaning: severe in punishment to him; or an explanation of the omitted apodosis, meaning: God will punish him, for indeed God is severe in punishment. In either case, the conditional clause completes what precedes it, confirms its content, and establishes the causal relation by way of demonstrative proof, as if it were said: that severe punishment is on account of their opposing God the Exalted and His Messenger, and whoever opposes God and His Messenger, whoever he may be, for him on account of that is a severe punishment. Therefore, for them, on account of their opposing both of them, there is a severe punishment. As for the claim that it is a threat to them with what has been prepared for them in the Hereafter after what has befallen them in this world, as has been said, it is refuted by what follows it, namely the words of the Exalted:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 14:

﴿That is, so taste it; and that for the disbelievers is the punishment of the Fire.﴾ For, together with the fact that it is the thing brought forward as a warning concerning what has been mentioned, it clearly indicates that the punishment meant in the verse is what befell them immediately. This holds whether (dhalikum, "that") is taken as a reference to the punishment itself, or to what the conditional clause implies regarding the establishment of punishment for them. As for the first case, the more evident view is that its grammatical position is accusative, governed by an implied verb demanded by His words, "so taste it." The waw in His words, "and that for the disbelievers..." etc., has the sense of (ma'a, "together with"). The meaning is: engage with that punishment which has struck you, so taste it immediately, together with the fact that for you is the punishment of the Fire later. The apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun in order to rebuke them for disbelief and to make it the cause of the ruling. As for the second case, the closer view is that its grammatical position is nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, and His words, "and that for the disbelievers..." etc., are coordinated with it. The meaning is: God's ruling is that, that is, the establishment of this punishment for you immediately, and the establishment of the Fire's punishment later.

His words, "so taste it," are a parenthetical insertion placed between the two coordinated elements for the purpose of threat. The pronoun refers, in the first case, to the very thing indicated, and in the second case, to what it contains. Various other views have been mentioned regarding the grammatical analysis of this noble verse, all of which revolve around the principle that the punishment meant is what struck them immediately. And God knows best. It was also read with a kasra on inna, as a new resumptive sentence.

O you who have believed, this is an address to the believers in a general rule that applies to whatever battles and encounters will occur. It was placed within the account (of Badr) to show concern for the matter and to strongly urge them to uphold it. ﴿When you meet those who have disbelieved advancing (zahf)﴾. Zahf is the crawling movement; it is said: "The child crawled (zahafa al-sabiyyu zahfan)" when he moved on his buttocks little by little. The term is applied to a massive army advancing toward the enemy, because due to its numbers and density it appears to be crawling, since the whole is seen as one connected body, so its movement is perceived, relative to its size, as extremely slow, even though in reality it is moving with the greatest speed. One of them said:

A huge host, like a mountain, you think they are standing still for a pilgrim's halt, while the riding beasts are pacing smoothly.

As for its being in the accusative, it may be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the object of (laqitum), meaning: advancing toward you. Or it may be a verbal noun (masdar) emphasizing a hidden verb of which it is the circumstantial clause, meaning: they advance in an advance. As for it being a circumstantial clause from its subject, or from both its subject and its object together, as has been said, this is rejected by His saying, ﴿So do not turn your backs to them﴾, since there is no sense in restricting the prohibition of turning one's back to their prior advance toward the enemy or to their large numbers. Rather, the enemy's advance toward them and their numerical superiority is what normally prompts retreat and necessitates the prohibition against it. Taking it to be an indication of what will happen from them on the day of Hunayn, when they turned their backs in flight while they were an advancing host of twelve thousand, is far-fetched. The meaning is: when you meet them in battle while they are many and numerous and you are few, do not turn your backs to them, let alone flee; rather, face them and fight them despite your fewness, let alone that you should approach them in number or equal them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 16:

﴿And whoever turns his back to them on that day﴾ — that is, the day of encounter — ﴿his back﴾, let alone fleeing. It is also read with the ba' sakin (﴿dubura﴾ read as ﴿dubrahu﴾ with a sukun on the ba'). ﴿Except one who swerves for battle﴾ — either by turning to fight another group more important than these, or by retreating in order to return to the attack (al-karr), by making the enemy imagine that he is defeated so as to deceive him and draw him out from among his helpers, then wheeling back upon him alone, or together with those of his companions who are in ambush. This is one of the stratagems and tricks of war. ﴿Or one who withdraws to a company﴾ — that is, one who joins another group of the believers in order to unite with them, and then fights the enemy alongside them.

On the authority of Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: A detachment (sariyyah) fled, and I was with them. When they returned to Madinah, they felt ashamed and entered their houses. I said: "O Messenger of Allah, we are the fleeers (al-farrarun)!" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Rather, you are the returners (al-'akkarun)." That is, the ones who attack again (al-karrarun), from 'akara, meaning he returned. "I am your company (fi'atukum)."

A man fled from al-Qadisiyyah and came to 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) in Madinah, saying: "O Commander of the Faithful, I was destroyed, so I fled from the battle line." 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "I am your company (fi'atuka)." The pattern of mutahayyiz is mutafay'il, not mutaf''il; otherwise it would be mutahawwiz, since it derives from hāza yajūzu. The two (mutaharrifan and mutahayyizan) are in the accusative either as circumstantial clauses (hal), with "illa" being superfluous and without governing effect; or as an exception from the ones who turn their backs, meaning: whoever turns his back to them, except a man from among them who is swerving or withdrawing. ﴿Then he has earned﴾ — that is, he returned ﴿with wrath﴾, a great wrath whose magnitude cannot be measured. The "min" in His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿from Allah﴾ is connected to an omitted element that serves as an attribute of "wrath," emphasizing what the tanwin conveys of grandeur and terror through the added grandeur: that is, with a wrath proceeding from Him, Exalted is He. ﴿And his refuge is Hell﴾ — that is, in place of the shelter he sought by fleeing, a refuge that would save him from being killed. ﴿And wretched is the destination﴾ — in placing the "bu'" (earning) in the position of the answer to the condition, which is the turning away, coupled with mention of the refuge and the destination, there is an eloquence beyond which nothing more can be added.

On the authority of Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both): fleeing from the battle line is among the greatest of the major sins, and this applies when the enemy is not more than double in number, based on His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿Now Allah has lightened [the burden] for you﴾ to the end of the verse. It has also been said that the verse is specific to the people of His household and those present with him in the battle.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 17:

﴿So you did not kill them﴾ is a return to explaining the remaining rulings and circumstances of the event and affirming what has preceded of them. The fa' (the particle "fa", here introducing a consequence) is the answer to an implied conditional clause, which is demanded by what has passed of the mention of God's reinforcement and His command to steadfastness and other things. It is as if it were said: "If the matter is so, then you did not kill them by your own strength and power, ﴿but God killed them﴾ through your victory and His empowering you over them and His casting terror into their hearts." It is also permissible that the implied meaning be: "If you know that, then you did not kill them," i.e., "know then," or "I inform you that you did not kill them." It has also been said that the implied meaning is: "If you boast of killing them, then you did not kill them," according to one of the two interpretations, because it is narrated that when they turned away from the battlefield victorious and laden with spoils, they came boasting, saying: "I killed, I captured, I did such and such, and I left such and such," and so this was revealed.

It has been narrated that "when Quraysh appeared from al-'Aqanqal, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'This is Quraysh, coming with its arrogance and its pride, denying Your Messenger. O God, I ask You for what You have promised me.'" Then Jibril (peace be upon him) came to him and said: "Take a handful of dust and throw it at them." When the two hosts met, he said to 'Ali (may God be pleased with him): "Give me a handful of pebbles from the valley," and he threw them into their faces and said, "May the faces be disfigured." No polytheist was left without being occupied with his eyes, and they fled. This is His statement, Mighty and Majestic, by way of the shifting of address: ﴿And you did not throw when you threw, but God threw﴾, affirming that the manifest throwing upon his hand (ﷺ) at that time was among His acts, Mighty and Majestic. The verb is stripped of its object because the primary aim is to explain the state of the throwing, by negation and affirmation, since it is that from which what appeared appeared, and it is the source of the change in what was thrown in itself and its multiplication to the point that a part of that reached the eyes of each one of that great community. That is: "And you, O Muhammad, did not perform that throwing with these great effects in reality when you performed it in form; otherwise its effect would have been of the kind of the effects of human actions. Rather, God performed it," i.e., created it when you engaged in it, but not in the manner of His usual practice in creating the actions of servants, rather in an unusual way. Therefore it had this effect which is beyond human capacity and the sphere of natural powers and destiny. So the basis for attributing it to God Most High and negating it from him (ﷺ) is that its effect is among his (ﷺ) actions. It was also read as (وَلَكِنِ اللَّهُ) with the lightened pronunciation and the nominative in both places. The lam in His statement, Most High: ﴿and that He might test the believers with it﴾, i.e., that He might give them from Him, Most High, ﴿a good trial﴾, i.e., a beautiful bounty not mixed with the endurance of hardships and adversities, is either connected to an omitted later element, so the waw is parenthetical, meaning: "and for the sake of benefiting them with victory and spoils He did what He did, not for anything other than that which would not benefit them;" or it is connected to (رَمى, "threw"), so the waw is conjunctive upon an omitted cause, meaning: "but God threw, in order to annihilate the disbelievers and in order to test ..." etc.

His statement, Most High: ﴿Indeed God is All-Hearing﴾, i.e., of their supplication and their pleading, ﴿All-Knowing﴾, i.e., of their intentions and their states that call for the answer, is a reason for the ruling.

"Dhalikum" refers to the good trial (al-bala' al-hasan), and its place in the i'rab is nominative, as the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'). His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and that Allah weakens the plot of the disbelievers﴾, with the genitive construction, is coordinated with it (ma'tuf 'alayhi). That is: the purpose is the testing of the believers, the weakening of the plot of the disbelievers, and the nullifying of their stratagems. It has also been said that what is referred to is the killing and the throwing, and the subject is "al-amr" (the matter), meaning: the matter is that, i.e., the killing. In that case, his saying, exalted is He, ﴿and that Allah...﴾ up to the end of the verse, is in the category of 'atf al-bayan (explicative apposition). It has also been read as "muwahhinun" with tanwin, both lightened and doubled (mukhaffafan wa mushaddadan), with "kayda" in the accusative (nasb).

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 8, verse 19:**

﴿If you seek a victory﴾ is addressed to the people of Makkah, in a mocking manner toward them. When they set out to leave, they clung to the curtains of the Ka'bah and said: "O God, give victory to the higher of the two armies, the better guided of the two groups, and the more honourable of the two parties." That is, "If you seek victory for the higher of the two armies," ﴿then there has come to you the victory﴾, in that He gave victory to the higher of them. You had claimed that you were the higher, so the mockery lies in the coming. Or it means ﴿there has come to you the defeat and subjugation﴾, so the mockery lies in the victory itself, since the term was used in place of its opposite. ﴿And if you desist﴾ from what you were engaged in of hostility and opposition to the Messenger (ﷺ), ﴿it is﴾, that is, desisting, ﴿better for you﴾, that is, than the hostility whose harm you have tasted, because in it there is safety from being killed or taken captive. The basis for considering the comparative good (ʿaṣl al-khayriyyah) in the thing preferred over is the mockery. ﴿And if you return﴾, that is, to hostility toward him (ﷺ), ﴿We shall return﴾, by giving you what you have witnessed of victory. ﴿And your company will not avail you at all﴾, read with the feminine ta' (tughni), though it is also read with the masculine ya' (yughni), because the feminine gender of fi'ah (group) is not real and because of the separation. That is, it will never repel from you ﴿your group﴾, your assembly which you gather and by which you seek help, ﴿anything﴾, that is, of benefit, or of harm.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿even though it be numerous﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumlah ḥāliyyah), and its verification has already passed. ﴿And that God is with the believers﴾, that is, and because God is the helper of the believers, that was so; or, the matter is that God is with the believers. Close to this in meaning is the reading with the kasrah (inna), on the basis of resumption (istiʾnāf).

It has been said: the address is to the believers, and the meaning is: if you seek victory, then victory has come to you; and if you desist from indolence and from the inclination away from what the Messenger (ﷺ) urges, then it is better for you than everything, because it is the means of attaining the happiness of both abodes. And if you return to it, We shall return to you with rejection and the stirring up of the enemy. Your numbers will then avail nothing if God is not with you in victory. The matter is that God is with those perfect in faith.

﴿O you who have believed, obey Allah and His Messenger, and do not turn away﴾ by omitting one of the two tā' letters, and it is also read with their assimilation (idgham, merging of one letter into the next) ﴿from him﴾, i.e., do not turn away from the Messenger. The intended meaning is the command to obey him and the prohibition of turning away from him. Mentioning obedience to Him, exalted is He, serves as a preparation (tamhid) and an alert (tanbih) that obeying Him is within obeying His Messenger (ﷺ): ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾. It is said that the pronoun refers to jihad, and it is said that it refers to the matter indicated by the word obedience. His statement, exalted is He, ﴿while you hear﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah) that comes to emphasize the obligation to cease from turning away absolutely, as in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿So do not set up rivals to Allah while you know﴾, not to restrict the prohibition to the state of hearing, as in His statement: ﴿Do not approach the prayer while you are intoxicated﴾. The meaning is: do not turn away from him while you are hearing the Qur'an, which speaks of the obligation to obey him, and the admonitions that restrain from opposing him, hearing with understanding and submission.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 21:

﴿And do not be﴾ is a confirmation of the preceding prohibition and a warning against opposing it, by alerting that such opposition leads to their being counted among the disbelievers, since their hearing becomes like not hearing at all. That is: do not be, by opposing the command and the prohibition, ﴿like those who said, "We hear,"﴾ by mere claim without understanding or acceptance, like the disbelievers and the hypocrites who claim to hear, ﴿while they do not hear.﴾ The phrase "while they do not hear" is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring back to the subject of "said." That is: they said that while the true state was that they do not hear, since they do not accept what they have heard, nor do they understand it as it should be understood, so it is as if they do not hear it at all.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 22:

﴿Indeed, the worst of living creatures﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), brought to explain the utter wretchedness of the state of those compared to them, as an intensification of the warning and a reinforcement of the prohibition following a previous reinforcement. That is: indeed the worst of what crawls upon the earth, or the worst of beasts, ﴿in the sight of Allah﴾, meaning in His judgment and decree, ﴿are the deaf﴾, who do not hear the truth, ﴿the dumb﴾, who do not speak it. They are described as deaf and dumb because the ear and the tongue were created for hearing the truth and speaking it; and since neither of these is found in them, they become as though they had lost both faculties altogether. The deaf are mentioned before the dumb because their deafness precedes their dumbness, for silence from speaking the truth is a branch of not hearing it, just as speaking it is a branch of hearing it. Then they are described as lacking reason, so it is said: ﴿who do not reason﴾, to affirm the utmost wretchedness of their state. For the deaf-mute who has reason may perhaps understand some matters and make others understand him by gesture, and guide himself thereby to some of his needs; but if he also lacks reason, then he is at the extreme of evil and wretched condition. By this it becomes evident that they are worse than beasts, since they have nullified that by which they are distinguished from them, and by which they are preferred over many of Allah's creatures, Mighty and Majestic is He; so they become baser than every base thing.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 8, verse 23:**

﴿And if Allah had known any good in them﴾, meaning some kind of good, part of which is directing their faculties toward seeking the truth and following guidance, ﴿He would have made them hear﴾ with the hearing of understanding and reflection. They would have stood by the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ), obeyed him, and believed in him. But He did not know any such thing in them, because they were entirely devoid of it. Thus He did not make them hear, since hearing would have been empty of benefit and outside of wisdom. To this the words of the Exalted refer: ﴿And if He had made them hear, they would have turned away﴾. That is, if He had made them hear with the hearing of understanding while they were in this state, utterly devoid of good, they would have turned away from the truth they heard and would never have benefited from it. Or, they would have apostatized after having affirmed it and become as though they had never heard it at all.

As for His words, the Exalted: ﴿while they were refusing﴾, it may be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the pronoun in "they would have turned away", meaning: they would have turned away on their backs while the state they were in was that they were refusing with their hearts what they had heard. Or it may be a parenthetical concluding clause (i'tirāḍ tadhyīlī), meaning: they are a people whose habit is refusal.

It was also said that they used to say to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Bring back Qusayy to life, for he was a blessed elder, so that he may testify for you and we may believe in you." The meaning then is: "And if He had made them hear the speech of Qusayy… etc."

It was also said that they were the sons of Abd al-Dar ibn Qusayy, of whom none became Muslim except Mus'ab ibn Umayr and Suwayd ibn Harmala. They used to say: "We are deaf, dumb, and blind to what Muhammad has brought; we do not hear it and we do not answer it." May Allah the Exalted fight them. They were all killed at Uhud, and they were the bearers of the standard.

It is related from Ibn Jurayj that they were the hypocrites (munafiqun). And it is related from al-Hasan (may Allah be pleased with him) that they were the People of the Book (Ahl al-Kitab).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 24:

﴿O you who have believed﴾ The repetition of the address, together with describing them by the attribute of faith, is to energize them toward eagerness to comply with the commands that follow it, and to alert them that within them is that which necessitates this. ﴿Respond to Allah and to the Messenger﴾ with good obedience ﴿when he calls you﴾, i.e., the Messenger, since he is the one directly carrying the call of Allah the Exalted ﴿to that which gives you life﴾ from the religious sciences, which are the locus of eternal life, just as ignorance is the cause of true death; or it is the water of the life of the heart, just as ignorance necessitates its death. It has also been said: [it is] for fighting the disbelievers, for if they abandoned it, they would overcome them and kill them, as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And in retribution there is life for you﴾.

It is narrated that he (ﷺ) passed by Ubayy ibn Ka'b while he was praying, and he called him, so he hastened in his prayer. Then he came and he (ﷺ) said: "What prevented you from answering me?" He said: "I was in prayer." He said: "Were you not told in what was revealed to me: ﴿Respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you﴾... etc.?" It is disputed concerning this. It has been said: this is one of the special features of his (ﷺ) call. It has been said: because his (ﷺ) response does not cut off the prayer. It has been said: that call was for a matter of importance that does not tolerate delay, and it is permissible for the one praying to cut off the prayer for the like of it.

﴿And know that Allah intervenes between a person and his heart﴾ is an image representing the extreme nearness of the Exalted to the servant, like His saying: ﴿And We are nearer to him than the jugular vein﴾. It is also an alert that He, the Exalted, is aware of the secrets of hearts, [including] what their owners may be heedless of; or it is an exhortation to hasten to sincerity of hearts and purifying them before the approach of death, for it intervenes between a person and his heart; or it is a depiction and imagining of His ownership over the servant's heart, such that He overturns his resolves, changes his intentions and aims, and comes between him and disbelief if He wills his happiness, and replaces his security with fear and his remembrance with forgetfulness, and similar of the obstructing matters that cause the opportunity to be lost.

It was read (بَيْنَ المَرِّ) with the doubling of the rāʼ, by dropping the hamza and placing its vowel on the rāʼ, and treating the connected form as the pause form. ﴿And that He﴾, i.e., Allah – Mighty and Majestic – or the matter ﴿to Him you will be gathered﴾, not to other than Him, so He will recompense you according to the degrees of your deeds. So hasten to the obedience of Him, the Exalted, and the obedience of His Messenger, and strive earnestly in responding to both of them.

Concerning Allah's words, ﴿And guard yourselves against a trial which will not strike exclusively those of you who have done wrong﴾: that is, its affliction is not confined to those among you who directly commit the wrong, but encompasses them and others, such as the tolerance of what is reprehensible (al-munkar) among you, compromising in enjoining good and forbidding what is reprehensible, the division of the community's word, the spread of innovations (bid'ah), and slackness in jihad (struggle in the way of Allah). Alternatively, His words ﴿will not strike﴾ ... etc. may be the response (jawab) to an imperative (al-amr), meaning: "If it strikes you, it will not strike [only] the wrongdoers..." etc. However, the response of the conditional (jawab al-shart) is uncertain, so the emphatic nun (nun al-ta'kid) is not appropriate for it, but since it carries the meaning of a prohibition (al-nahy), its use is permissible, as in the words of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿Enter your dwellings, lest Solomon and his hosts crush you﴾. Or it may be an attribute (sifah) of "trial" (fitnah), and not of the negation; but this is anomalous (shudhudh), because the nun does not enter a negated verb except in an oath. Or it is a prohibition with the sense of "saying" implied, like the words of one who said:

"Until, when darkness fell and mingled, they came with a thin drink; did you ever see the wolf?"

Or it is the response to an omitted oath (qasam), as in the recitation (qira'ah) of one who read (la-tusibanna), although the meanings of the two differ. It has also been permitted that it be a prohibition against approaching wrongdoing after the command to guard against sin, for its consequence (wabal) strikes the wrongdoer alone and returns upon him. The "min" in "minkum" is partitive (lil-tab'id) according to the first possibilities, and explanatory (lil-tabyin) according to the last two. Its benefit is to draw attention to the fact that wrongdoing by you is more hideous than wrongdoing by others. ﴿And know that Allah is severe in punishment﴾, and for this reason He afflicts with punishment those who did not directly commit its cause.

﴿And remember when you were few﴾: that is, at the time when you were few in number. The choice of the nominal sentence (al-jumla al-ismiyya, a sentence beginning with a noun rather than a verb) indicates the continuation of the state they were in: the fewness, and what follows from it of weakness and fear. The words of the Exalted, ﴿oppressed﴾, are a second predicate (khabar) or an adjective (sifa) of ﴿few﴾. The words ﴿in the land﴾ mean: in the land of Makkah, under the hands of Quraysh, and the address is to the Muhajirun (the emigrants). Or [it means]: under the hands of Persia and Byzantium, and the address is to the Arabs as a whole, for they were humiliated under the hands of the two powers.

The words of the Exalted, ﴿fearing that the people might snatch you away﴾, are a third predicate, or a second adjective of ﴿few﴾, described by a sentence after being described by a single word. Or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun hidden in ﴿oppressed﴾. By "the people," according to the first view, which is the more apparent, is meant either the disbelievers of Quraysh, or the disbelievers of the Arabs, because of their proximity to them and the intensity of their hostility toward them. According to the second view, it is Persia and Byzantium. That is: remember the time of your fewness, your humiliation, your lowliness among the people, and your fear of being snatched away by them.

﴿So He sheltered you﴾ in Madinah, or made for you a refuge in which you could protect yourselves from your enemies. ﴿And strengthened you with His help﴾ against the disbelievers, or through the support of the Ansar, or through the reinforcement of the angels. ﴿And provided for you of the good things﴾, namely the spoils of war. ﴿So that you may give thanks﴾ for these magnificent blessings.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 8, verse 27:**

﴿O you who have believed, do not betray Allah and the Messenger﴾. The root meaning of *khawn* (betrayal) is deficiency, just as the root meaning of *wafa'* (fulfilment) is completeness. Its use for the opposite of *amanah* (trustworthiness) is because betrayal includes that deficiency. That is, do not betray them both by neglecting the obligatory duties (*fara'id*) and the recommended practices (*sunan*), or by concealing the opposite of what you openly show, or by *ghulul* (misappropriation) of the spoils of war.

It is narrated that he (ﷺ) besieged Banu Qurayza for twenty-one nights, and they asked for terms of peace, just as he had made peace with Banu al-Nadir on the condition that they would depart to their brethren at Adhri'at and Ariha in Syria. He refused except that they submit to the judgment of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh (may Allah be pleased with him). They refused and said: "Send us Abu Lubaba," who was their advisor, because his property and family were in their hands. So he sent him to them. They said: "What do you think, should we submit to the judgment of Sa'd?" He gestured towards his throat, meaning that it is slaughter. Abu Lubaba said: "My feet had not moved until I knew that I had betrayed Allah and His Messenger." Then this verse was revealed. He tied himself to one of the pillars of the mosque and said: "By Allah, I will not taste food or drink until I die or Allah accepts my repentance." He remained for seven days until he fell unconscious. Then Allah accepted his repentance. It was said to him: "You have been forgiven, so release yourself." He said: "No, by Allah, I will not release myself until the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is the one who releases me." So he (ﷺ) came and released him. He said: "Indeed, part of the completeness of my repentance is that I abandon the house of my people in which I committed the sin, and that I divest myself of my wealth." He (ﷺ) said: "A third is sufficient for you to give in charity."

﴿and do not betray your trusts﴾ among yourselves. It is *majzum* (in the jussive mood) and *ma'tuf* (conjoined) to the first, or it is *mansub* (in the accusative mood) as an answer following the conjunction *wa* (and). ﴿while you know﴾ (p-18) that you are betraying, or that you are people of knowledge who distinguish the good from the evil.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 28:

﴿And know that your wealth and your children are only a trial﴾ because they are a cause of falling into sin and punishment; or they are a test from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, by which He tries you in them, so let not their love lead you to betrayal, as with Abu Lubaba. ﴿And that with Allah is a great reward﴾ for the one who prefers His good pleasure, may He be exalted, over them both, and observes His limits concerning them. So direct your aspirations toward that which will lead you to it.

O you who believe! (Repetition of the address and the attribute of faith serves to show the utmost care for what follows, and to signal that it is among the things that faith requires one to observe and guard, as in the two preceding addresses.)

﴿If you fear Allah﴾, i.e., in what you do and what you refrain from, ﴿He will grant you﴾ as a result of that ﴿a criterion (furqan)﴾: guidance in your hearts, by which you distinguish truth from falsehood; or victory that separates the one who is right from the one who is wrong, through the exaltation of the believers and the humiliation of the disbelievers; or a way out of doubts; or deliverance from what you fear in both abodes; or a manifestness that makes your affair famous and spreads your renown, from the saying: "I spent the night doing such-and-such until the furqan dawned," i.e., the morning (ṣubḥ). ﴿And will expiate from you your misdeeds﴾, i.e., will cover them, ﴿and will forgive you﴾ your sins by pardon and overlooking them. It has been said: the misdeeds (sayyi'at) are the minor sins and the sins (dhunub) are the major sins. It has also been said: what is meant is what preceded and what follows, because this verse was revealed concerning the people of Badr, and Allah the Exalted has forgiven both for them.
