His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah is the Possessor of great bounty﴾ is a reason (ta'lil) for what precedes it, and an alert that what Allah the Exalted promised them in return for taqwa is a bounty and a kindness from Him, not something that taqwa necessitates, just as when a master promises his servant a reward for a deed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 30:

﴿And [recall] when those who disbelieved were plotting against you﴾ is in the accusative as an object (maf'ul) governed by a suppressed verb addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, conjoined to His saying, exalted is He: "And remember when you [were few]..." etc. It is brought to remind [him] of the special blessing upon him ﷺ after the reminder of the general blessing for all. That is: "And remember the time of their plotting against you" ﴿to confine you﴾ with chains, which is supported by the reading of those who read (liyuqayyidukа, "to shackle you"), or [to inflict] severe wounding, from their saying: "He struck him until he rendered him immobile, with no movement in him and no escape," and it was read (liyuthabbitūka) with the shaddah, and (liyubayyitūka) from al-bayt (night attack). ﴿Or kill you﴾, that is, with their swords; ﴿or expel you﴾, that is, from Makkah. This was because, when they heard of the Ansar's embracing Islam and their pledge to him ﷺ, they were alarmed and gathered in the Dar al-Nadwa to consult about his affair ﷺ. Iblis entered upon them in the form of an old man and said: "I am from Najd; I heard of your gathering and wanted to attend, and you will not lack from me an opinion and counsel." Abu al-Bukhturi said: "My opinion is that you imprison him in a room, seal its exits except for a small opening through which you pass him his food and drink, until he dies." The old man said: "Evil is that opinion; his people will come to fight you and rescue him from your hands." Hisham ibn 'Amr said: "My opinion is that you place him on a camel and take him out of your land, and then what he has done will not harm you." He said: "Evil is that opinion; it will corrupt other peoples than you and fight you with them." Abu Jahl said: "I see that you take from every clan a youth and give him a sword, and they strike him one blow together, so his blood is scattered among the tribes, and the Banu Hashim will not be able to fight all of Quraysh. Then, if they demand the blood-money, we will pay it." He said: "This young man has spoken truly," and they dispersed upon his opinion. Then Jibril came to the Prophet, peace be upon them both, and informed him of the news, and commanded him to emigrate. So he had 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, sleep in his bed, and he went out with Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, to the cave.

﴿And they plot, and Allah plots﴾, that is: He turns their plotting back upon them, or requites them for it, or deals with them in the manner of those who plot. This was by bringing them out to Badr and making the Muslims appear few in their eyes, until they charged against them and met with what they met.

﴿And Allah is the best of plotters﴾: He does not heed their plotting when He plots, and attributing such things to Him, glorified is He, is permissible for the sake of mushakalah (correspondence of wording), but it is not permissible to begin with it, because it gives the impression of what does not befit Him, glorified is He.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 31:

﴿And when Our verses are recited to them﴾ which ought to make the mountains of solid rock prostrate before them, ﴿they say: "We have indeed heard. If we wished, we could say the like of this."﴾ This was said by the accursed al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, and its attribution to all of them is because he was their chief and their judge, whose word they followed and whose opinion they adopted. It is also said: it was said by those who conspired concerning his matter ﷺ in Dar al-Nadwa (the assembly house of Quraysh). And this, as you see, is the utmost of obstinacy and the extreme of stubborn opposition. How could it not be so? For if they had been able to do anything of that sort, what was preventing them from the attempt? They had been challenged for ten years, were confronted with their incapacity, and tasted from that the bitterest of experiences; then they were confronted with the sword, yet they did not oppose it with anything else, despite their pride and their great aversion to being overcome, especially in the domain of eloquence. ﴿This is nothing but the fables of the ancients﴾, i.e., what they write down of stories.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 32:

﴿And when they said: "O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment."﴾ This too is among the falsehoods of that accursed one (al-La'in, i.e., Abu Jahl).

It has been narrated that when he said, "This is nothing but the fables of the ancients," the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Woe to you! It is the speech of Allah, the Exalted," and so he said that. The meaning is: if the Qur'an is indeed the truth, sent down from You, then rain down upon us stones as a punishment for our denial, or bring upon us some other painful punishment. What is intended by this is mockery (tahakkum) and the display of certainty and complete conviction that it is not so, far be it (from the Qur'an) to be so. It has also been read as "al-haqqu" in the nominative, with "huwa" being a subject (mubtada') and not a pronoun of separation (fasl). The benefit of the definite article here is to indicate that what is conditioned upon it is being the truth in the manner he claims (ﷺ), namely that it is sent down, not the truth absolutely, since they allowed that it might correspond to reality without being sent down, like the fables.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 33:

﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them.﴾ This is a response to their shameful utterance, and an explanation of what necessitates His deferring their punishment and withholding the answer to their supplication. The lam (lam of emphasis) serves to reinforce the negation and to indicate that their punishment would be a punishment of annihilation (isti'sal) — while the Prophet (ﷺ) is among them — would be outside of His usual practice (ʿadah), and not consistent with His judgment and decree. As for their seeking forgiveness mentioned in His words, ﴿And Allah would not punish them while they seek forgiveness⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿—⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿ ⁠﻿﻿ the intended meaning is either the seeking of forgiveness by those among the believers who remained among them, or their saying, "O Allah, forgive (us)," or it is understood as a conditional sense: if they were to seek forgiveness, they would not be punished, like His words, ﴿And your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly while their people are reformers⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿—⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿⁠﻿﻿ ﻿﻿⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿⁠

﴿Why should Allah not punish them?﴾ This explains that they deserve punishment, after having shown that the obstacle does not come from them. That is, what do they have that would prevent their being punished once that obstacle is removed? And how could they not be punished? ﴿While they bar [people] from the Sacred Mosque﴾: that is, while this is their condition, including their barring [the Muslims] when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was driven to emigrate (al-Hijrah) and their blockade of him in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah. ﴿And they were not its guardians﴾: this is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause, in Arabic ḥāl, a grammatical term for a phrase describing the condition of the subject at the time of the action) referring back to the pronoun in "they bar," and it conveys the full ugliness of what they did in barring. Their direct act of barring [people] from it, while not being entitled to authority over its affairs, is supremely ugly. This is also a refutation of their claim: "We are the custodians of the House and the Sanctuary, so we bar whom we wish and admit whom we wish." ﴿Its guardians are only the God-fearing﴾, those who are free from shirk (polytheism, Arabic shirk), who do not worship anyone besides Him, exalted is He. ﴿But most of them do not know﴾ that they have no authority over it. This implies that some of them know this but are obstinate. It has also been said that by "most of them" is meant all of them, just as "few" is sometimes used to mean "none."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 35:

﴿And their prayer at the House was nothing but whistling and clapping.﴾ That is: their supplication, or what they call prayer, or what they put in the place of prayer. ﴿Nothing but mukā'an﴾, that is, whistling. It is fu'āl from makā, yamkū, when one whistles (ṣaffara). It has also been read with shortened vowel as bukan, like al-buka (weeping). ﴿Wa-taṣdiyatan﴾, that is, clapping: it is taf'ilah from al-ṣadā (echo), or from al-ṣadd (turning away), with one of the two doubled letters replaced by a yā'. It has also been read (ṣalātahum) in the accusative, so that it is the predicate of (kāna), and the thrust of the statement is to establish that they deserve punishment, or that they have no right of guardianship over the Masjid, since such prayer does not befit one whose prayer is this.

It is reported that they used to circumambulate the House naked, men and women alike, interlacing their fingers, whistling through them and clapping. It was also said: they used to do this when the Prophet ﷺ intended to pray, confusing him, and imagining that they themselves were praying too.

﴿So taste the punishment﴾, that is: killing and capture on the day of Badr. It was also said: the punishment of the Hereafter. The lām in (al-'adhāb) may be for previous reference (al-'ahd), and the referent is their saying, "Bring us a painful punishment." ﴿Because you used to disbelieve﴾, both in belief and in deed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 36:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve spend their wealth to avert [people] from the way of Allah﴾. It was revealed concerning those who provided food on the day of Badr. They were twelve men from Quraysh, each of whom fed, every day, ten camels (judur). Or it was revealed concerning Abu Sufyan, who hired two thousand [men] for the day of Uhud, apart from those he recruited from among the Arabs, and spent forty awqiyya on them. Or it was revealed concerning the companions of the caravan: when Quraysh was struck on the day of Badr, it was said to them, "Help against the war on Muhammad with this wealth, so that perhaps we may obtain our vengeance from him," and they did so. By "the way of Allah" is meant His religion and following His Messenger.

﴿So they will spend it﴾ in full. Perhaps the first [spending] is a report about their spending in that situation, which is the spending of the day of Badr, and the second is a report about their spending in what is yet to come, which is the spending of the day of Uhud. It is also possible that both refer to one [event], on the basis that the context of the first is to explain the purpose of the spending, and the context of the second is to explain its outcome and that it has not yet occurred.

﴿Then it will become for them a source of regret﴾: remorse and grief at its loss without attaining the intended aim. He made the very [spending] a regret, which is its outcome, for emphasis. ﴿Then they will be overcome﴾ in the end, although the war between them was back and forth (sijal) before that.

﴿And those who disbelieve﴾, i.e., they persisted in disbelief and insisted upon it, ﴿will be gathered to Hell﴾, i.e., they will be driven [there], not to anywhere else.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 37:

﴿That He may distinguish the wicked from the good﴾. That is: the disbeliever from the believer, or corruption from righteousness. The lam (preposition "that/in order that") is connected to "yuhsharun" (they will be gathered), or to "yughlabun" (they will be overcome), or to what the polytheists spent in their enmity towards him (ﷺ) of what the Muslims spent in his support. The lam is connected to His saying, "then it will be a regret for them." It is also read as "liyumayyiza" with the intensive doubling (tashdid) for emphasis (mubalagha).

﴿And will place the wicked, some of it upon others, and heap it all together﴾. That is: He joins some of it to others, until they pile up because of the intensity of their crowding, so He gathers it together; or He adds to the disbeliever what he spent, in order to increase his punishment, as it is for the disbelievers, ﴿and will put it into Hell﴾, all of it.

﴿Those﴾ is a reference to "the wicked," since it is an expression for the group, or to the spenders. The meaning of distance in it (the demonstrative with distance) is to signal the distance of their rank in wickedness. ﴿They are the losers﴾, the complete ones in loss, because they lost their souls and their wealth.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 38:

﴿Say to those who disbelieve﴾ They are Abu Sufyan and his companions; that is, say this for their sake. ﴿If they desist﴾ from what they are engaged in of opposing the Prophet (ﷺ), by entering into Islam, ﴿their past sins will be forgiven for them﴾. It is also read as (in tanhawu yughfar lakum) and (yaghfir lakum) in the active voice, the agent being Allah, exalted is He. ﴿But if they return﴾ to fighting them, ﴿then the precedent of the former peoples has already passed﴾, those who banded together against the Prophets, peace be upon them, through scheming, as happened to the people of Badr. So let them expect the like of that.

"And fight them" is conjoined to "Say" (in the preceding verse), and the address has been generalized to increase the believers' eagerness for fighting, so as to realize what His words (Exalted is He), "the way of the former peoples has already passed" [8:38], include of the threat: ﴿until there is no more fitnah﴾, i.e., no polytheism (shirk) remains among them, ﴿and the religion is entirely for Allah﴾, and the false religions vanish, either by destroying all their adherents or by their turning away from them out of fear of being killed.

﴿But if they desist﴾ from disbelief through your fighting, ﴿then indeed Allah is Seeing of what they do﴾, so He will reward them for their desisting from it and their accepting Islam. It is also read with the second-person ta' (of address), meaning: "of what you do" of the striving (jihad) that brings them out to Islam. Making it dependent on their desisting serves to indicate that they are rewarded through causation, just as those who directly perform the act are rewarded for the act itself.

﴿And if they turn away﴾ and do not desist from that, ﴿then know that Allah is your Mawla (Protector)﴾, your Helper. So rely upon Him and do not care about their hostility toward Him. ﴿How excellent is the Protector﴾, who does not abandon whoever takes Him as protector, ﴿and how excellent is the Helper﴾, who is not overcome whoever He helps.

(p-22)﴿And know that whatever you obtain as spoils﴾. Al-Kalbi reported that it was revealed concerning Badr. Al-Waqidi said: the khums (one-fifth) was prescribed in the expedition of Banu Qaynuqa', a month and three days after Badr, on the middle of Shawwal, at the twentieth month after the Hijra. "Ma" is a relative pronoun (mawsula), and its returning pronoun is omitted, meaning: "that which you seized from the disbelievers by force (ʿanwatan)." The root meaning of ghanima (spoils) is obtaining sheep (ghanam) from the enemy; then the term was broadened and applied to whatever is obtained from them, whatever it might be. His words, Exalted is He, ﴿of anything﴾ are an explanation of the relative pronoun, and its grammatical position is accusative, as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the returning pronoun of the relative clause. It is intended to emphasize the importance of the spoils and that nothing should escape from them. That is: whatever you have taken as spoils, of anything that falls under the designation "thing," even a thread or a needle, except that the slayer's spoils (salab) go to the slayer if the Imam grants them to him as a special reward (nafl), and that prisoners are subject to the Imam's choice, and likewise the conquered lands.

As for His words, Exalted is He, ﴿then to Allah belongs its fifth﴾: it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted, meaning: "then it is a right or an obligation that to Him, Exalted is He, belongs its fifth." This clause is the predicate of "li-annama" (because) ... etc. It has also been read with a kasra (fa-inna), and the first reading is more emphatic and stronger in obligation, because of the repetition of the predication, as if it were said: "There must be a fixed fifth, and there is no way to neglect it." It has also been read (fa-lillahi khumusuhu), and read (khumsahu) with a sukun on the mim. The majority hold that the mention of Allah, Exalted is He, is for glorification, as in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿and Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾, and that the intended meaning is the division of the fifth among those who are mentioned after it in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿and to the Messenger, and to the near of kin, and the orphans, and the needy, and the wayfarer﴾. The repetition of the particle "li" before "dhi al-qurba" (the near of kin), but not before the other three categories, is to remove the assumption that they share in the portion of the Prophet (ﷺ), because of their closer connection to him (ﷺ). They are the Banu Hashim and the Banu al-Muttalib, but not the Banu Abd Shams or the Banu Nawfal, based on what has been reported from Uthman and Jubayr ibn Mut'im, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "These are your kinsmen, the Banu Hashim. We do not deny their merit, because of your position which Allah has placed you among them. But what about our brethren, the Banu al-Muttalib? You have given to them and withheld from us, while we and they are in one and the same station." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "They have not separated from us in the Jahiliyya or in Islam; indeed, the Banu Hashim and the Banu al-Muttalib are one thing," and he interlaced his fingers. As for the manner of its division according to us, it was during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in five shares: one share for him (ﷺ), one share for the mentioned near relatives, and three shares for the remaining three categories. As for after him (ﷺ), his share lapses, and likewise the share of the near relatives; they are given only because of their poverty, so they are like the rest of the poor, and their wealthy are not given. It is then divided among the three categories. This is supported by what has been reported from Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, that he withheld the khums from the Banu Hashim and said: "What is due to you is only that your poor are given, your unmarried women are married, and those among you who have no servant are provided with one. As for everyone else, he is like the wealthy wayfarer, who is not given anything from the alms."

It is also reported from Zayd ibn Ali the same, and he said: "It is not lawful for us to build palaces from it, nor to ride thoroughbred mounts from it." It was also said: the share of the Messenger (ﷺ) goes to the ruler (wali al-amr) after him.

As for al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, it is divided into five shares: one share for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), spent on what he (ﷺ) used to spend on the interests of the Muslims, such as equipping the warriors with horses and weapons and the like; one share for the near relatives, rich and poor among them, divided among them so that the male receives the equivalent of the portion of two females; and the remainder for the three remaining categories.

(p-23) As for Malik, may Allah have mercy on him: the matter is entrusted to the ijtihad (independent judgment) of the Imam. If he sees fit, he divides it among these groups; if he sees fit, he gives some of them and not others; and if he sees another category more deserving and more important, then it goes to them.

Abu al-Aliya relied on the apparent meaning of the noble verse and said: it is divided into six shares, and the share of Allah, Exalted is He, is spent on the door-ring (ritaj) of the Ka'ba, based on what has been reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to take a handful from it and place it toward the needs of the Ka'ba; then he divides what remains into five shares. It was also said: the share of Allah goes to the public treasury (bayt al-mal). It was also said: it is added to the share of the Messenger (ﷺ). This is the status of the khums. As for the remaining four-fifths, they are divided among the warriors (ghanimun): for the foot soldier one share, and for the horseman two shares, according to Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him; and three shares according to the two of them (Abu Yusuf and al-Shaybani), may Allah have mercy on them both.

Al-Qurtubi said: When Allah, Exalted is He, explained the ruling on the khums and remained silent about the rest, this indicates that the remainder is the property of the warriors.

As for His words, Exalted is He, ﴿if you have believed in Allah﴾: it is connected to an omitted element indicated by what has been mentioned, meaning: "If you have believed in Him, Exalted is He, then know that the khums of the spoils must be given as a means of drawing near to Allah, Exalted is He, so cut off your desires from it and be content with the four-fifths." The intended meaning is not mere knowledge of this, but knowledge accompanied by action and obedience to His command, Exalted is He. ﴿And what We sent down﴾ is coordinated with the sacred Name, meaning: "if you have believed in Allah and in what We have sent down ﴿upon Our servant﴾." It has also been read ("ʿubudinā"), which is a collective noun, and by it is meant the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers, since some of what was sent down was sent down upon them directly, as you will know. ﴿On the day of the Criterion﴾: the day of Badr, so named because it distinguished between truth and falsehood. It is in the accusative governed by "anzalna" or by "amantum." ﴿The day the two hosts met﴾: that is, the two groups of believers and disbelievers. It is either a substitute for "the day of the Criterion" or in the accusative governed by "al-Furqan." What is meant is what was sent down upon him (ﷺ) on that day of revelation, angels, and victory, with the sending down understood as mere conveyance and facilitation, so that everything is included in a true sense. Belief in the sending down of these things was made one of the necessary grounds for knowing that the khums belongs to Allah, Exalted is He, in the manner mentioned, since the revelation clearly states this, and since the angels and the victory came from Him, Exalted is He, it is required that what was obtained through them as spoils be spent on the causes that Allah, Exalted is He, has specified. ﴿And Allah is over all things competent﴾: He is able to grant victory to the few over the many, and the humble over the mighty, as He did for you on that day.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 42:

﴿When you were on the nearer side of the valley﴾ is a second substitute (badal) for ﴿the Day of Criterion﴾. The ʿudwah (ʿudwa) — with a ḍammah — is the bank of a valley; likewise with a fatḥah or a kasrah, and it has been read with each of them as well. ﴿And they were on the farther side﴾, i.e., the far side from Madinah. It is the feminine of al-aqsa, and the analogical form would have been to change the waw into a yaʾ, as in al-dunya and al-ʿulya, even though both are from the waw-root; but it came in its original form, as in al-qawad, and it was deemed correct (istusşwiba). It is more commonly used than al-quṣya. ﴿And the caravan﴾, i.e., the trade caravan or its leaders, ﴿was lower than you﴾, i.e., in a place lower than your place, meaning the coast. It is in the accusative as an adverb of place (ẓarfiyyah), occupying the position of the predicate, and the sentence is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the adverb before it. Its benefit is to indicate the strength of the enemy and their reliance on the caravan, and their eagerness to fight to protect it, and the settling of their souls on not leaving their positions and exerting their utmost effort, and the weakness of the Muslims' condition and the precariousness of their affair, and the improbability of their victory by ordinary custom. Likewise is the mention of the positions of the two parties, for the nearer side was (p-24) soft, where feet would sink and one could not walk without hardship, and there was no water in it, unlike the farther side. Likewise is His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And if you had made an appointment together, you would have differed about the appointment﴾, i.e., if you and they had agreed upon fighting, then you had known your state and their state, you would have differed among yourselves about the appointment out of awe of them and despair of victory over them. So that they would be certain that the victory which came to them was nothing but a deed from Allah, mighty and majestic, which breaks customary norms, and so they would increase in faith and gratitude, and their souls would be reassured by the prescription of the khums. ﴿But﴾ He brought you together in this state without an appointment ﴿so that Allah might accomplish a matter that was destined to be done﴾, truly deserving to be carried out — the granting of victory to His friends and the subduing of His enemies — or one predetermined from eternity.

And His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿That whoever perishes might perish upon clear evidence, and whoever lives might live upon clear evidence﴾ is a substitute for it, or it is connected to "accomplished" (maf'ulan), i.e., that whoever dies should die upon a clear proof he witnessed, and whoever lives should live upon a clear proof he observed, so that there would be no argument or excuse for him, for the event of Badr was among the manifest signs; or so that the disbelief of him who disbelieves and the faith of him who believes would proceed from clarity of evidence, using the metaphor of perishing and living for disbelief and faith. By "whoever perishes" and "whoever lives" is meant those who are on the verge of perishing and living, or whose state in the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, is perishing and living. It has been read as (liyahlaka) with a fatḥah, and (wa-ḥayiya) with the disassimilation of the doubled letter, treating it as the future.

﴿And indeed Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾, i.e., of the disbelief of him who disbelieves and his punishment, and the faith of him who believes and his reward. Perhaps the combination of the two attributes is because both matters involve speech and belief.

The verse ﴿When Allah showed them to you in your dream as few﴾ is in the accusative case, governed by "اذْكُرْ" (remember), or it is another substitute (badal, a word that replaces and clarifies the earlier noun) for "يَوْمَ الفَرْقانِ" (the Day of Criterion), or it is connected to "عَلِيمٌ" (Knowing). That is, He knows what is beneficial, when He makes them appear few in your eyes in your dream. Telling your companions of this would strengthen them and encourage them against their enemy.

﴿And if He had shown them to you as many, you would have lost heart﴾, meaning you would have become cowardly and shrunk from advancing. ﴿And you would have disputed about the matter﴾, meaning the matter of fighting, and your opinions would have scattered between standing firm and fleeing. ﴿But Allah saved [you]﴾, meaning He granted safety from failure and dispute. ﴿Indeed, He is Knowing of what is in the breasts﴾, He knows what will be in them of boldness, cowardice, patience and despair, and for this reason He arranged what He arranged.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 44:

﴿And when He showed them to you, when you met, as few in your eyes﴾ is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb addressed to all of them by way of shifting address and generalization (taltin wa-ta'mim), and coordinated with the earlier implied pronoun. The two pronouns are the objects of (yurі, "He showed") and (qalilan, "few") is a circumstantial accusative (hal) referring to the second. He made them appear few in the eyes of the Muslims to such an extent that Ibn Mas'ud - may Allah be pleased with him - said to the one beside him: "Do you see them as seventy?" He said: "I see them as a hundred," in order to strengthen them and to confirm the dream of the Messenger (ﷺ).

﴿And He made you appear few in their eyes﴾ to such an extent that Abu Jahl said: "The companions of Muhammad are only men who eat camel meat." He made them appear few in their eyes before the fighting clashed, so that they would become bold against them and not prepare for them; then He made them appear numerous, so that they saw them as twice their number, so that the abundance would take them by surprise, and they would be dumbfounded and fearful. This is among the great signs of that encounter, for the eye may see the many as few and the few as many, but not in this manner and not to this extent. It was only by Allah the Exalted turning the sights away from seeing some while not others, despite equality in the conditions (p-25).

﴿That Allah might accomplish a matter that was to be done﴾ is repeated because the verb that it is connected to differs, or because the intended "matter" there is the meeting in the aforementioned manner, while here it is the exaltation of Islam and its people and the humiliation of unbelief and its party. ﴿And to Allah all matters are returned﴾, all of them; He directs them however He wills, none can repel His command, none can avert His judgment, and He is the Wise, the Glorious.

O you who have believed! When you encounter a company (fi'ah) [of the disbelievers], then stand firm, and remember Allah much, that you may succeed.

Abu al-Su'ud, Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim:

The address is introduced with the two particles of calling and alerting (harfay al-nida' wa-al-tanbih), to show the complete care given to what follows. "When you encounter" (idha laqitum) means: when you fight a group of the disbelievers (kafara). They are not described as disbelievers here because it is evident that the believers fight only disbelievers. "Encounter" (al-liqa') is among the terms that have come to signify fighting (ghalaba fi al-qital). "Then stand firm" (fa-uthbutu) means: for their encounter in the places of battle. "And remember Allah much" (wa-udhkuru Allaha kathira) means: amid the fighting, drawing strength from Him, seeking His help, relying upon His remembrance, and awaiting His victory. "That you may succeed" (la'allakum tufliphun) means: that you may attain your aim and achieve your desired outcome of victory and reward. In this there is an admonition that the servant should not let anything occupy him from the remembrance of Allah the Exalted, that he should turn to Him in times of hardship, and that he should come to Him wholeheartedly, free of mind, confident that His kindness never leaves him in any state whatsoever.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 46:

﴿And obey Allah and His Messenger﴾ in all that you do and all that you refrain from, so that what they were commanded here is included in it by way of primary inclusion (indirajan awwaliyyan). ﴿And do not dispute﴾ over differing opinions, as you did at Badr or Uhud. ﴿Lest you falter﴾ is the answer (jawab) to the prohibition; it was said that it is coordinated (ʿatf) with it. ﴿And your strength depart﴾ is in the accusative (bi-l-nasb), coordinated with the answer to the prohibition, and it was read in the jussive (bi-l-jazm), on the assumption that "fa-tafshalu" is coordinated with the prohibition. That is, your dynasty (dawlah) and your might (shawkah) will go away. The word (rih, "wind") is used here metaphorically for dynasty, inasmuch as the affair's progress and its enforcement are likened to the blowing and flowing of the wind. It was also said that the intended meaning is literal, for victory comes only by a wind that Allah Most High sends. And in a hadith: "I was made victorious by the eastern wind (al-sabā), and ʿĀd were destroyed by the western wind (al-dabbūr)."

﴿And be patient﴾ in the hardships of war. ﴿Indeed, Allah is with the patient﴾ through victory and protection. What is understood from the word (maʿa, "with") regarding their being the originators is only in that they are the ones who directly practise patience, so they are followed from that aspect; and Allah's being with them is only in terms of support and assistance.

﴿And do not be like those who went forth from their homes﴾ after they had been commanded with what they were commanded of the best of deeds, and forbidden what is opposed to them of their ugly deeds. By them is meant the people of Makkah when they went forth to protect the caravan, ﴿insolently﴾, i.e., with boasting and exultation, ﴿and to be seen by people﴾, so that they would praise them for courage and generosity. When they reached al-Juhfah, a messenger of Abu Sufyan came to them and said: "Turn back, for your caravan has been saved." But they refused except to display the signs of steadfastness, so they suffered what they suffered, as was mentioned at the beginning of this noble surah. Thus the believers were forbidden to be like them, showing off and being insolent, and they were commanded to have piety and sincerity, inasmuch as the prohibition of a thing necessarily implies the command to its opposite.

﴿And they bar from the way of Allah﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with *baṭaran* (بَطَرًا), if it is taken as a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the position of the *ḥāl* (circumstantial accusative, a word describing the state of the subject at the time of the action), and likewise if it is taken as an object of purpose (*mafʿūl lahu*), but with the verbal noun interpreted as a verb of purpose. ﴿And Allah is encompassing of what they do﴾, so He will recompense them for it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 48:

﴿And [remember] when Satan made their deeds seem fair to them﴾ is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb addressed to the Prophet ﷺ by way of tilwin (shifting of address), i.e.: "And remember the time when Satan made their deeds seem fair to them in opposing the believers and otherwise, by whispering to them ﴿and said, "No one among the people can overcome you today, and I am your protector."﴾" That is: he cast into their hearts and imagined to them that they could not be overcome nor could they be withstood, because of the greatness of their number and their equipment, and he made them think that their following him, in what they assumed to be acts of devotion, was a protection for them, so that they said: "O Allah, give victory to the better of the two parties, and to the better of the two religions." And (lakum) is the predicate of (la ghaliba) or its attribute, and not its complement, for otherwise it would be in the accusative, as in your saying: "No one striking Zayd is with us."

﴿So when the two hosts came in sight﴾ — that is, when the two groups met — ﴿he turned back on his heels﴾ — he retreated backward, i.e.: his scheming came to nothing, and what had been imagined to them as their protector became the cause of their destruction. ﴿And he said, "I am innocent of you. I see what you do not see. I fear Allah."﴾ That is: he disowned them, feared for them, and despaired of their condition when he saw Allah, the Exalted, reinforcing the Muslims with angels. It has been said: when the Quraysh gathered to set out, they recalled the enmity between them and Kinanah, which nearly deterred them, so Iblis appeared to them in the form of Suraqah ibn Malik al-Kinani and said: "No one among the people can overcome you today, and I am your protector against Kinanah." When he saw the angels descending, he turned back. He had his hand in the hand of al-Harith ibn Hisham, who said to him: "Where are you going? Will you abandon us in this situation?" He said: "I see what you do not see," and he pushed al-Harith in the chest and departed, and they fled. When they reached Makkah, they said: "Suraqah has routed the people," and this reached him, and he said: "By Allah, I had no awareness of your march until your defeat reached me." When they became Muslims, they knew that it had been Satan. In light of this, the meaning of his saying "I fear Allah" may be: I fear that He will strike me with some harm from the angels, or destroy me; and the time would be the time promised, when he saw in it what he had not seen before. The first (interpretation) is what al-Hasan said, and Ibn Bahr preferred it. ﴿And Allah is severe in punishment﴾ — this may be part of his speech, or a new statement from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 49:**

﴿When the hypocrites say﴾ is in the accusative case, governed by (*zayyana*, "made fair-seeming"), or by "*nakasa*" (turned back), or by "*shadid al-'iqab*" (severe in punishment). ﴿And those in whose hearts is a disease﴾ means: those whose hearts have not yet come to rest in faith, and in which some degree of doubt remains. It has also been said that they are the polytheists, and it has been said that they are the hypocrites in Medina. The conjunction (*'atf*) is used because the two descriptions differ, as in his saying:

؎ Alas for Zayyaba, for al-Harith, the one who rises at dawn, then the one who gains booty, then the one who returns.

﴿Their religion has deluded these﴾ means the believers, ﴿their religion﴾, to the point that they exposed themselves to what they had no power to face. So they went out, three hundred and some ten, against about a thousand. ﴿And whoever relies upon Allah﴾ is a reply to them from Him, exalted is He, and a rebuttal of their statement. ﴿Then indeed Allah is Mighty﴾, dominant, who does not humiliate whoever relies upon Him and seeks refuge in Him, even if he is few. ﴿Wise﴾, He acts by His far-reaching wisdom in ways that minds find improbable, and in understanding which the intellects of the discerning are bewildered. The answer to the conditional is omitted, because what has been mentioned indicates it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 50:

﴿And if you could see﴾ That is: and if you (O Muhammad) saw. For "law" of impossibility (law al-imtina'iyya) turns the present tense into the past, just as "in" (in) turns the past into the present. The address is either to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) or to everyone who is fit to be addressed. Its verification has already been discussed in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And if you could see when they are made to stand over the Fire﴾. The word "idh" (when) in His words, exalted is He: ﴿when the angels take the souls of those who disbelieve﴾ is an adverbial clause of time (zarf) for "you see" (tara), and the object is omitted. That is: and if you saw the disbelievers, or the state of the disbelievers, when the angels take their souls at Badr. The fronting of the object is for emphasis on it. It has also been said: the agent is a pronoun referring back to God, Mighty and Majestic, and "the angels" is the subject (mubtada'), and His words, exalted is He: ﴿striking their faces﴾ are its predicate (khabar), and the clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the relative pronoun, in which the pronoun has been used in place of the conjunction "wa" (and). According to the first view, it is a circumstantial clause from the object, or from the angels, or from both of them, because it contains pronouns referring to both.

﴿and their backs﴾ That is: and their buttocks, or what faced them and what turned away from them of the body parts. ﴿And taste the punishment of the burning﴾ on the assumption of an implied "saying" (qawl), coordinated with "striking" (yadribun), or as a circumstantial clause from its agent. That is: and they say, or saying: Taste. It is a glad tiding to them of the punishment of the Hereafter. It has also been said: they had with them rods of iron, and whenever they struck, the fire flared up from them. The answer to "law" (if) is omitted, to signal that it goes beyond the limits of description. That is: you would see a dreadful matter that can scarcely be described.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 51:**

﴿That﴾ is a reference to what was mentioned of the striking and the punishment, and the sense of distance in it (the demonstrative) indicates that the two are at the furthest extreme of terror and awfulness. It is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is ﴿because of what your hands have sent forth﴾. That is, that striking and punishment befall you by reason of what you earned of disbelief and disobedience. The position (mahall) of "anna" (that) in His words ﴿and that Allah is not ever unjust to the servants﴾ is nominative (raf'), as the predicate of a deleted subject (mubtada' mahdhuf). That is: "and the matter is that He, exalted is He, does not punish His servants without sin on their part." Expressing this by negating injustice, even though punishing them without sin is certainly not injustice, according to the established principle of the People of the Sunnah (ahl al-Sunnah, the Sunni tradition of creed), let alone being gross injustice, has already been verified in the commentary on surah Al 'Imran. The clause is a concluding parenthetical (i'tiradi tadhyili, a clause placed at the end to confirm what precedes it), confirming the meaning of what comes before it. As for what has been said, that it is coordinated (ma'tufah) upon what precedes, to indicate that its causal role is restricted by its being joined to it, since without it He could have punished them without their sins, it is not sound. This is because the possibility of His punishing His servants without sin, indeed its actual occurrence, does not contradict the punishment of these specific disbelievers being due to their sins, such that one would need to consider its absence alongside it. Yes, if the claim were that all of His punishments are due to the sins of those punished, then that would need to be considered.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 52:

﴿As with the people of Pharaoh﴾ is in the nominative position, as the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada'), and the clause is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) brought to explain that what befell them of punishment was due to their disbelief and not to anything else from outside them, by likening their condition to the condition of those known for destruction because of their crimes, in order to increase the reproach of their state. It also serves as an alert that this is a constant practice (sunnah muttarida) among the destroyed nations; that is: their custom which they persisted in, of the deeds they committed and of the seizing that was done to them, "as with the people of Pharaoh," who were well known for the ugliness of their deeds and the severity of the punishment and retribution.

﴿And those before them﴾ that is: before the people of Pharaoh, from the nations who committed the sins they committed and met the punishment they met, such as the people of Noah, 'Ad and their likes among the people of disbelief and obstinacy.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿disbelieved in the signs of God﴾ is an explanation of their custom which they practised, not of the custom of the people of Pharaoh and their likes, as has been said, for that is understood from it by virtue of the comparison. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so God seized them﴾ is an explanation of their custom which was done to them, and the fa' (so) is to show that it is among the necessary consequences of their crimes and their results which follow from them. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿for their sins﴾ serves to emphasise what the fa' conveyed of causation, along with an indication that they had, in addition to their disbelief, other sins which had a part in bringing about the punishment. It is also permissible that the intended meaning of "for their sins" is their acts of disobedience which follow from their disbelief, in which case the ba' indicates accompaniment; that is: He seized them while they were involved in their sins, not repenting of them. So their custom is the whole of what they did and what was done to them, not merely what they did, as has been said.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: The people of Pharaoh were certain that Musa, peace be upon him, was a prophet of Allah, yet they denied him; likewise these people: Muhammad (ﷺ) came with the truth and they denied him, so Allah sent down upon them His punishment, just as He sent it down upon the people of Pharaoh. Making the punishment part of their custom, although it is not the kind of thing whose constant recurrence and habituation by them can be imagined, as is required in the meaning of "custom" (da'b), is either by way of giving precedence to what they did over what was done to them, or by treating their constant persistence in what entails disbelief and disobedience as equivalent to their constant persistence in the punishment itself, because of the complete connection between the two. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Mighty, severe in punishment﴾ is a parenthetical clause (i'tiradh) confirming the content of what precedes it of the seizing, and his saying, exalted is He:

Ibn Abi Hatim is not cited here, so I translate only the given text.

﴿That﴾ ... etc. is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) brought to give the reason for what the noble structure implies: that the punishment which befell them was tied to their evil deeds, not occurring without a prior cause requiring it. What is pointed to is not the very punishment and retribution that befell them, as some have said. For even though it is the thing being explained, by their disbelief and sins mentioned above, it cannot be explained by the continuous custom of God Most High not to change a blessing He has bestowed upon a people until they change their own condition. The assumption that the cause is not what is mentioned, as the explicit wording of the noble structure states, but rather what is derived from the implication of the limit (mafhum al-ghayah), namely the continuous custom of God Most High of changing their blessing when they change their condition, on the basis of the imagined idea that the punishment is the effect of their disbelief without any exception, is a grave error, a departure from the truth by a great distance, a belittling of the matter of disbelief in the signs of God, and a removal of it from the rank of making punishment obligatory in a context meant to magnify it and warn against it. So the meaning is: "That," i.e., the punishment was consequent upon their evil deeds, rather than occurring at the outset, although God is capable of that.

﴿Because God﴾, i.e., because of the fact that He, Exalted is He, ﴿was not﴾ in Himself ﴿one who changes a blessing He has bestowed﴾, i.e., it was not fitting for Him, glorified is He, nor proper in His wisdom, that He should be such that He would change a blessing He had bestowed ﴿upon a people﴾ of the peoples, whatever blessing it was, great or small, ﴿until they change what is in themselves﴾ of deeds and states in which they were at the time they enjoyed the blessing, and take on what contradicts it, whether their prior states were pleasing and righteous, or close to righteousness relative to the event, like the case of these disbelievers, who before the mission were disbelievers, worshippers of idols, persisting in a state that warranted the bestowal upon them of the blessing of respite and all the other worldly blessings. When the Prophet ﷺ was sent to them with clear signs, they changed it into something worse and more displeasing to God, as they denied him ﷺ, opposed him and those of the believers who followed him, and banded together against them, seeking to harm them. So God Most High changed the blessing of respite He had bestowed upon them, and hastened punishment and chastisement upon them. The original form of "yakun" is "yakunu," and the nun was dropped for lightness, due to its resemblance to the soft letters.

﴿And that God is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾: a conjunction with "that God..." etc., falling together with it within the scope of the reason, i.e., and because God Most High is All-Hearing and All-Knowing, He hears and knows all that they do and leave undone of statements and actions, past and future, and therefore orders upon each of them what befits it, of preserving or changing the blessing. It is also read "wa-inna Allah" with a kasra on the hamza; in that case the sentence is a resumptive clause affirming the content of what precedes it. And the words of God Most High:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 54:

﴿Like the custom of the people of Pharaoh and those before them﴾. It is in the accusative position (mahall al-nasb), as a qualifier (na't, adjective) of an omitted verbal noun (masdar), meaning: "until they change what is in themselves, a change like the custom of the people of Pharaoh," i.e., like their change, on the basis that their custom (da'b) is an expression only for what they did, as is most appropriate to the concept of da'b. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿They denied the signs of their Lord﴾, is an explanation of it in its entirety. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So We destroyed them﴾, is a report of the consequence of punishment being due upon it, not that it is part of its explanation. There is no harm in the placement of His saying, exalted is He, "And that Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing" between them, as its parallel was mentioned in Surat Al 'Imran, where they permitted the accusative position of the kaf (the particle "like") with (lan tughniya) despite what is between them of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And those are the fuel of the Fire﴾. This is according to the assumption that the sentence is joined to what precedes it. As for the assumption that it is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD), there is absolutely no objection to its placement in between. It was also said: it is in the nominative position, as the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), as before it. The sentence then becomes another resumptive clause (isti'naf), brought to confirm what the first resumptive clause was brought for, by comparing their custom with the custom of those mentioned, but not by way of pure repetition (takrir), rather by changing the heading, and making da'b on both sides an expression of what necessarily accompanies its first meaning, namely the change of condition and the change of blessing, taking this from what His saying, exalted is He, expressed: ﴿That is because Allah never changed a blessing﴾ up to the verse. That is: the custom and the affair of these people, which is an expression of the two mentioned changes, is like the custom of those, when they changed their condition, so Allah, exalted is He, changed His blessing upon them. So His saying, exalted is He, ﴿They denied the signs of their Lord﴾ is an explanation of their custom which they did, of their changing their condition. And His saying, exalted is He, (So We destroyed them) is an explanation of their custom which was done to them, of His changing what was upon them of His blessing. As for the custom of Quraysh, it is derived from it by way of the comparison. How excellent is the manner of the revelation, in that it sufficed, in each of the two comparisons, with explaining one of the two sides. The addition of the signs (ayat) to the Lord, which is attached to the pronoun (hum), is for increasing the reprehensibility of what they did to them of denial. The shift (iltifat) to the nun of majesty (nun al-'azama) in (ahlakna) follows the customs of greatness, in order to magnify the gravity of the matter. The discussion concerning the fa' and concerning His saying, exalted is He, ﴿because of their sins﴾ is like what has passed. The conjunction of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And We drowned the people of Pharaoh﴾ to (ahlakna), despite its being included under it, is to indicate the complete horror and atrocity of drowning, like the conjunction of Jibril (peace be upon him) to the angels. ﴿And all﴾, i.e., and all of the mentioned groups, or all of these and those, or all of the drowned Copts and the slain of Quraysh, ﴿were wrongdoers﴾, i.e., wronging themselves through disbelief and sins, since they exposed them to destruction, (p-30) or placing disbelief and denial in the place of faith and affirmation, and for this reason there befell them what befell them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 55:

﴿Indeed, the worst of creatures﴾ Having explained the conditions of those among the worst of the disbelievers who were destroyed, he (Abu al-Su'ud) proceeded to explain the conditions of the rest of them and the detailed rulings concerning them. His words, Exalted is He, ﴿with Allah﴾ meaning: in His judgment and decree, ﴿are those who disbelieved﴾ meaning: those who persisted in disbelief and obstinately clung to it, were made the worst of living creatures (dawabb, "creatures that walk on the earth") rather than the worst of people; this is an indication that they are far removed from being of the same kind as humankind, and that they are in fact of the kind of beasts, yet worse than all of its individuals, as His words, Exalted is He, expressed: ﴿They are only like cattle; rather, they are even more astray﴾. His words, Exalted is He, ﴿so they do not believe﴾ are a ruling that follows from their persistence in disbelief and their being firmly rooted in it, and a declaration concerning them that they are of the very nature of sealing (of hearts), so that no turning-away diverts them and no inclination bends them at all. It is placed in the manner of a parenthetical interjection (i'tiraD), not as a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon "disbelieved," since it is included together with it within the scope of the relative clause (silah), in which no ruling is made by the verb. His words, Exalted is He:

"Those with whom you made a covenant" (alladhina 'ahadta minhum) is a substitute (badal) for the first relative pronoun, or an explicative apposition (‘atf bayan) to it, or in the accusative by way of censure (nasb 'ala al-dhamm), meaning: you made a covenant with them. The word "min" (from) serves to indicate (li-l-iydhan) that the covenant-making, which is an expression for giving and receiving a pledge from both sides, is considered here with regard to his (ﷺ) taking their pledge, since it is the basis for the ugliness of the breach that is censured in them, not his (ﷺ) giving them his pledge. It is as if it were said: "Those from whom you took their pledge." It has also been said that "min" is for partitive meaning (li-l-tab'id), because those who directly undertake the pledge are some of them, not all of them.

"Then they break their covenant" ('ataf 'ala 'ahadta) is conjoined to "you made a covenant," falling together with it under the ruling of the relative clause (hukm al-silah). The present-tense form (sighat al-istiqbal) indicates the renewal and repetition of the breach, and that they are of this intention at all times. That is: they break their covenant which you took from them "every time" (fi kulli marrah), meaning: of the occasions of making a covenant, since these are the occasions in which non-breach is expected and its occurrence is considered abhorrent, not of the occasions of war, as has been said, since in those occasions non-breach is not expected; rather it is not even conceivable at all, such that its occurrence would be considered abhorrent, because those occasions are the likely occasions for its absence. Therefore there is no benefit in restricting the breach to occurring at each of the occasions of war, and indeed it is categorically invalid; for the breach is only realized in the occasion following the covenant, not in the occasions occurring afterward without a covenant. And even if it is granted that what is meant is the occasions occurring immediately after the covenant, the breach occurring without war, such as selling weapons and the like, remains outside the explanation. And even if that is counted as war, there is no escape from the consequence that the speech is entirely devoid of benefit; for war in this sense is identical with breach, so the matter comes down to saying: "They break their covenant at every occasion of breaking," and interpreting "war" as war against others, so that the meaning becomes: "They break their covenant at every occasion of war against the enemies" — though this is extremely remote and weak — entails that their initiating the breach falls outside the explanation.

"While they do not fear (la yattaqun)" is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "yanqudun" (they break), meaning: they persist in breaking, and the state is that they do not guard against the disgrace of treachery, and they do not mind the shame and the Fire that it entails. As for the words of the Exalted:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 57:

﴿Then if you gain the upper hand over them in war﴾ This begins the explanation of their rulings after the detailing of their conditions. The fa' (fa, "then") indicates the sequence of what follows upon what precedes, i.e., if their state is as mentioned, then if you encounter them and gain mastery over them (p-31) ﴿in war﴾, meaning: in the midst of it.

﴿so disperse those behind them﴾ meaning: scatter, away from your opposition to them, with a harsh dispersal that compels them to flight and disorder, and make an example of them by inflicting upon them such punishment and torment as will cause others to take warning. (Tankil, "making an example," is the act of inflicting such punishment that it deters.)

﴿who are behind them﴾ meaning: those of the disbelievers who are behind them. This implies that they are poised for war, being near to these people. It is also read (sharrid) with the dhal pointed, and it is perhaps a metathesis of (shadhdhir), meaning "scatter." It is also read (min khalfihim), meaning: carry out the dispersal from behind them. The meaning is one, because the infliction of dispersal upon those behind them is not realized except by dispersing those who are behind them.

﴿so that they may take heed﴾ that they may be admonished by what they witnessed of what befell those who broke the covenant, so that they refrain from breaking it, or from disbelief. And His, exalted is He, saying:

And if you fear treachery from a people ﴿وَإمّا تَخافَنَّ مِن قَوْمٍ خِيانَةً﴾ is an explanation of the rulings concerning those who are about to break the covenant, following the explanation of the rulings concerning those who have already broken it in practice. The word "fear" is used figuratively (isti'ara, metaphorical usage) for "knowledge." That is: and if you come to know, of a people among the covenanted, that they will break the covenant in the future, through the signs of treachery and the indications of evil that have appeared to you from them, ﴿then throw back to them﴾, meaning: cast their covenant back at them, ﴿on equal terms﴾, meaning: on a straight and even path, by openly showing them the breach and informing them plainly that you have cut off what was between you and them of the bond. Do not engage them in war while they still assume the covenant remains, so that there may be no trace of treachery on your part at all.

The prepositional phrase "on equal terms" is connected to a omitted element, which is a circumstantial clause (hal) describing the one doing the throwing back. That is: then throw back to them while standing firm on equal terms. It was also said: on equality in knowledge of the breach of the covenant, such that both the furthest and the nearest of them are equal in it, or such that you and they are equal in it. According to the first view, it is a circumstantial clause describing those to whom the covenant is returned; according to the second, it describes both parties.

﴿Indeed, Allah does not love the treacherous﴾ is a justification (ta'lil) for the command to throw back the covenant. It is either in view of its implying a prohibition on engaging in combat, which is itself treachery, so it serves as a warning to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) against it; or in view of its entailing fighting afterward, so it serves as an incitement to him (ﷺ) to throw back the covenant first and then to fight them second, as if it had been said: and if you come to know of treachery from a people, then throw back to them, then fight them, for Allah does not love the treacherous, and they are among them, given what you know of their condition.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 59:

﴿And let not those who disbelieve suppose﴾ i.e., themselves; the object has been omitted because it is repeated (in the sense that it is understood from the context). His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿that they have outstripped﴾, i.e., have escaped and eluded being overpowered, is the second object of (yahsabanna, "let them suppose"). The intended meaning is to make them despair of deliverance and to sever their vain hopes of benefiting from the rejection (of the treaty), and to limit (the statement) to repelling this delusion. This is so because resisting the believers, or even overcoming them, is something on which their false wishes depend; the purpose is to alert (the reader) that this is not something their imagination or supposition even approaches, and that what can occur to their minds is only the supposition of finding a way out. It has also been said: the verb is ascribed to someone (unspecified), or to (those behind them), and the first object is the relative pronoun, which includes them as well. It has also been said: it is the subject, and "that" (an) is omitted before (sabaqu, "they have outstripped"), and it together with what falls within its scope takes the place of both objects. The sense is: "And let not those who disbelieve suppose that they have outstripped." This is reinforced by the reading of one who read (annahum sabaqu, "that they have outstripped"). A parallel for this omission is His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿And of His signs is that He shows you the lightning, as a fear﴾, and His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿Do you order me to worship other than Allah?﴾ and the verse (continues). This was said by al-Zajjaj.

It was also read with the (second person) ta' (tahsabanna, "you suppose"), addressing the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this reading is clear. It was also read (wa la tahsabi alladhina, "and do not suppose those who"), with the bā' vowelled with kasra and with fatha, on the omission of the light nun (nun al-tawkid al-khafifa). His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿Indeed they cannot escape (innahum la yu'jizun)﴾, i.e., they will not get away, and their pursuer will not find himself unable to overtake them; it is an explanation of the prohibition in the manner of a resumed statement (isti'naf). It was also read with the hamza vowelled with fatha (annahum la yu'jizun), on the omission of the lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil). It has also been said: the verb has the pronoun as its object, "la" is superfluous, and (sabaqu, "they have outstripped") is a circumstantial clause (hal) in the sense of (sabiqin, "outstripping"), i.e., escaping and fleeing. This (interpretation) is according to the reading in the second person, to remove what might be feared regarding the consequence of the rejection, since it is an alerting of the enemy and an enabling of them to flee and to escape from the hands of the believers. In it is the negation of their capacity to resist and to confront, in the most eloquent and emphatic manner, as has been indicated. It has also been said: it was revealed concerning whoever escaped from the rout of the polytheists. It was also read (la yu'jizuni, "they will not frustrate me") with the nun vowelled with kasra, and (la yu'ajjizuni, "they will not frustrate me") with the doubled ja'.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 8, Verse 60:**

﴿And prepare against them﴾: The address is directed to all the believers, because the commanded act is among the duties of everyone. Likewise, the address in what precedes and follows it is directed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, because what falls within his sphere is among his duties (ﷺ). That is, prepare to fight those with whom the covenant has been repudiated and make ready your weapons for them. Or it means to fight the disbelievers in general, which is the more suitable reading given the context of the noble verse. ﴿whatever you can of strength﴾: of everything by which one can strengthen oneself in war, whatever it may be.

It is related on the authority of ʿUqba ibn ʿAmir, may Allah be pleased with him: I heard him ﷺ say on the pulpit: "Indeed, strength is archery. Indeed, strength is archery. Indeed, strength is archery." He said it three times. Perhaps the Prophet's ﷺ singling out of archery for mention is because it surpasses its counterparts among the forms of strength.

﴿and of steeds of war﴾: *al-Ribāṭ* (the horses kept tethered for war) is a term for the horses that are tethered in the way of Allah, the Most High. It is either a *fiʿāl* form in the sense of a *mafʿūl* (i.e., "that which is tethered"), or a verbal noun by which the horses themselves were named. One says *rabata rabṭan wa ribāṭan*, and *rābaṭa murābaṭatan wa ribāṭan*. It may also be the plural of *rabīṭ*, like *faṣīl* and *fiṣāl*, or the plural of *rabṭ*, like *kaʿb* and *kaʿāb*, and *kalb* and *kilāb*. It has been read as *rubuṭi al-khayl* with the *bāʾ* vowelled with a *ḍamma* and also with sukūn, being the plural of *ribāṭ*. Its coordination with "strength," although it is part of that strength, serves to indicate its excellence over the rest of its kinds, like the coordination of Gabriel and Michael with the angels.

﴿by which you strike terror into﴾: that is, you frighten. It has been read *turahhibūna* with the doubling of the letter *rāʾ*, and *tukhzūna bihi* (with *khazā*). The pronoun refers either to *mā istaṭaʿtum* or to the preparation, and the latter is more suitable. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from the subject of *aʿiddū* (prepare), meaning: "Prepare while striking terror by it," or from the relative pronoun, or from its omitted resumptive pronoun, meaning: "Prepare what you are able to do, striking terror by it."

﴿the enemy of Allah and your enemy﴾: they are the disbelievers of Mecca. They are singled out from among the disbelievers, even though all of them are such, because of the extent of their rebelliousness and their exceeding of bounds in enmity. ﴿and others besides them﴾: others among the disbelievers. It was said that they are the Jews; it was said that they are the hypocrites; it was said that they are the Persians. ﴿whom you do not know﴾: that is, you do not recognize them by their persons, or you do not know them in the state of enmity they are in. The latter is more suitable in view of His, the Most High's, words: ﴿Allah knows them﴾, that is, none other than Him does, for their persons are known to others besides Him, the Most High, as well.

﴿And whatever you spend of anything﴾ for the preparation of equipment, be it little or much, ﴿in the way of Allah﴾, which jihad makes clear, ﴿will be repaid to you﴾: that is, its reward will be given to you in full. ﴿and you will not be wronged﴾ by withholding the reward or by annulling the recompense. The expression of withholding it as "wronging," even though deeds do not necessarily entail reward such that withholding its bestowal would be a wrong, serves to demonstrate the perfect purity of Him, glorified be He, from such a thing, by portraying it in the form of something that is impossible for Him, the Most High, to commit among the ugly acts. The presentation of the granting of reward in the guise of matters obligatory upon Him, the Most High, is as has passed in the explanation of His, the Most High, words: ﴿So their Lord responded to them: "Indeed, I will not allow to be lost the work of any worker among you"﴾ (3:195).

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 61:**

﴿And if they incline to peace﴾. Al-junuh (inclination) means leaning, and from it comes al-janah (wing). It is construed with al-lam and with ila. That is: if they incline ﴿to peace﴾, i.e., to reconciliation, with dread falling into their hearts upon witnessing the preparedness and the readiness of arms that you possess. ﴿Then incline to it﴾ (p-33), i.e., to peace. The feminine pronoun is used because (the word) is treated as the opposite of war, as the poet said:

Peace: take from it whatever pleases you, while war suffices you with a few sips of its breaths.

It is also read as (fajnuh), with a damma on the nun.

﴿And put your trust in Allah﴾, and do not fear that they will show you peace while their inner hearts are folded over deceit and treachery. ﴿Indeed He﴾ (exalted is He) ﴿is the All-Hearing﴾, so He hears what they say in their private gatherings of deceptive speech, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾, so He knows their intentions, and holds them accountable for what they deserve, and turns their plotting back upon their own necks. The verse is specific to the Jews. It was also said that it is general, and that it was abrogated by the verse of the sword.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 62:

﴿And if they intend to deceive you﴾ by displaying peace and abandoning hostility, ﴿then sufficient for you is Allah﴾, i.e., know that the one who suffices you (Muhsibaka, "the one who reckons for you") against their evils and the one who helps you against them is Allah. ﴿It is He who supported you with His help﴾ is a justification for His sufficiency for him (ﷺ), presented as a resumptive clause (isti'naf), since His support for him (ﷺ) in the past, in the manner mentioned, from the improbable outcomes, is among the proofs of His support in what will come later. That is: it is He who supported you with aid from Him directly, without intermediary, as in His saying, ﴿And victory is not except from Allah﴾, or through the angels, along with His breaking of customary patterns (kharq al-'adat). ﴿And with the believers﴾ from among the Muhajirun (Emigrants) and the Ansar (Helpers).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 63:

﴿And He joined their hearts together﴾ along with what had existed between them before that of tribal zealotry (ʿaṣabiyya), rancour (ḍaghīna), and an eagerness for vengeance (tahālluk ʿalā al-intiqām), to such a degree that scarcely could two hearts among them come together, until, by His divine grant of success (tawfīq), they became as one soul. This is among the most dazzling of his ﷺ miracles. ﴿Even if you had spent all that is on earth, all of it﴾, meaning: for the purpose of joining them together, ﴿you could not have joined their hearts together﴾. This is a resumptive clause (istiʾnāf) that confirms what precedes it and clarifies the rarity of the aim and the difficulty of achieving it. That is: their enmity had reached such a limit that, even if a spender had expended in the reconciliation of their affairs (iṣlāḥ dhāt al-bayn) all the wealth and treasures that are on earth, he would not have been able to bring about the joining and reconciliation. The mention of "hearts" serves to indicate that joining them together is not attainable, even if outward union is possible.

﴿But God joined them together﴾, both heart and body, by His overwhelming power. ﴿Indeed He is Mighty﴾, possessing complete power and dominance, such that nothing He wills is beyond Him. ﴿Wise﴾, knowing how to subject to His will whatever He desires.

It is said: the verse concerns the Aws and the Khazraj, among whom there were endless grudges and battles that wiped out their chiefs and their great men, and smashed their necks and skulls. God, Mighty and Majestic, caused them to forget all of that and joined them together through Islam, until they became sincere friends, shooting from one bow and becoming helpers (anṣār).

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 8, verse 64:**

﴿O Prophet﴾. This begins an explanation of Allah's sufficiency for him (ﷺ) in all of his affairs and the affairs of the believers, or in the matters between them and the disbelievers in general, following an explanation of His sufficiency for him (ﷺ) in a particular matter. The sentence is introduced with the vocative particle and the alerting particle (ḥarfay al-nidāʾ wa-l-tanbīh) to draw attention to the greater importance of its content. Mentioning him (ﷺ) by the title of prophethood indicates that this title is the reason (ʿillīyah) for the ruling. ﴿Allah is sufficient for you﴾, that is, He suffices you in all your affairs, or in what lies between you and the disbelievers of warfare. ﴿and those who follow you of the believers﴾ occupies a place in the accusative case, as an object of accompaniment (mafʿūl maʿahu), meaning: Allah suffices you and suffices your followers as a helper, as in the words of the one who said:

*"Then sufficient for you and al-Ḍaḥḥāk is a keen Indian sword."*

It was also said that it occupies a place in the genitive case, as a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on the pronoun, which is the view of the Kufans, meaning: He suffices you and those who suffice you. Or it occupies a place in the nominative case, as a conjunction on the name of Allah, the Exalted, meaning: Allah suffices you and the believers. The verse was revealed in the desert (al-Bayda') during the Battle of Badr, before the fighting. It was also said that thirty-three men and six women embraced Islam with the Prophet (ﷺ), and then ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) embraced Islam, and so it was revealed. For this reason Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: It was revealed concerning the conversion of ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him).

﴿O Prophet﴾. After having explained that He suffices him with victory and reinforcement, he (ﷺ) was commanded to arrange the principles of his victory and reinforcement. The repetition of the address in the aforementioned manner (ﷺ) serves to show the complete care given to the matter he was commanded to carry out.

﴿Urge the believers to fight﴾. That is: exert yourself in exhorting them to it and encouraging them to it, by every means possible among the encouraging matters, the greatest of which is reminding them of God's promise of victory and His judgment that He suffices them, or that they suffice (themselves) with Him.

The root of tahrid (incitement, urging on) is ḥaraḍ, which is that illness wears a person down until he nearly dies. Al-Raghib (al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī) said: "It is as if, originally, it is the removal of ḥaraḍ, which is that which has no good in it and is not counted." I say: the more apparent view, then, is to take ḥaraḍ as an expression for weakness of heart, which is of the kind of the wasting caused by illness. It was also said: the meaning of urging them is calling them ḥaraḍ, by saying: "I see you in this matter as ḥaraḍ," that is, one who urges on in it, because of its stirring them to advance. It was read as (ḥarriṣ) with the unpointed ṣād, and this is clear.

﴿If there are twenty steadfast among you, they will overcome two hundred﴾. This is a generous promise from Him, the Exalted, of the overcoming of every group of believers over ten times their number, by way of istinaf (resumption, a new independent sentence) after the command to urge them. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if there are a hundred among you, they will overcome a thousand﴾, although its meaning is understood from what precedes it, since each of the two is a number based on the support of one over ten, is for the sake of increased confirmation, which yields increased reassurance, because it may happen between two small groups what does not happen between two large groups, while the difference between each of the two small groups and the two large groups is in one and the same ratio. So He made clear that this does not differ in the two cases.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from among those who disbelieved﴾ is an explanation of "the thousand." This restriction is also to be taken into account for the two hundred, and its mention has been omitted, relying on its mention here, just as the restriction of steadfastness has been omitted here although it is necessarily to be taken into account, relying on its mention there.

﴿because they are a people who do not understand﴾. It is connected to (they will overcome). That is: because they are a people ignorant of God, the Exalted, and of the Last Day, who do not fight seeking reward and obeying the command of God, the Exalted, and exalting His word, and seeking His good pleasure, as the believers do. Rather, they fight out of jahiliyya zeal (ḥamiyya jāhiliyya, pagan tribal zeal) and following the footsteps of Satan, and stirring up the flame of transgression and aggression. So they deserve nothing but subjugation and humiliation.

As for what has been said, that whoever does not believe in God and the Last Day does not believe in the promise, so happiness for him is nothing but this worldly life, and so he is stingy with it and does not expose it to loss by engaging in wars and plunging into the sources of calamities, and so he inclines to what contains safety, and so he flees and is overcome. And as for whoever believes that there is no happiness in this transient life, and that happiness is only the enduring life, he does not care for this worldly life and does not give it any weight, and so he advances to jihad with a strong heart and a sound resolve, and so one of such a man stands in the place of many. This is a true statement, but it does not suit the context.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 66:

(p-35) ﴿Now Allah has lightened [the burden] for you, and He knows that there is weakness in you.﴾ Since the preceding promise implied the obligation for one to resist ten and to stand firm against them, as is reported from Ibn Jurayj, that it was incumbent upon them not to flee and for one to stand against ten, and [since] the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had sent Hamzah with thirty riders, and he met Abu Jahl with three hundred riders, and he defeated them; it was burdensome for them, and they complained about it after a period, so it was abrogated (nusikha) and lightened for them by making one resist two. It is also said: there was a scarcity of them at the beginning, then when they became many, the lightening was revealed. What is meant by "weakness" is weakness of body. It is also said: weakness of insight, for they varied in being guided to fighting, not weakness in religion, as has been said. It was also read as (ḍu'fan) with a ḍamma on the ḍād, and this is a dialect of the same word, like faqr and fuqr, and makth and mukth.
