It is also said: ḍa'f with a fatḥa is what pertains to opinion and intellect, and ḍu'f with a ḍamma is what pertains to the body. It was also read as (ḍu'afā') the plural of ḍa'īf. As for what is meant by His knowledge of their weakness, it is His knowledge of it in terms of it being realized in fact, not His knowledge of it absolutely; how could it not be so, since that is established from eternity?

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So if there are among you a hundred steadfast, they will overcome two hundred﴾, it is an explanation of the lightening and a clarification of its manner. It was read (takun) here and in what preceded with the upper ta (tā' fawqāniyyah).

﴿And if there are among you a thousand, they will overcome two thousand by the permission of Allah﴾, i.e., by His facilitation and making easy. This qualification ("by the permission of Allah") is operative in what preceded regarding the overcoming of a hundred over two hundred and of a thousand, and the overcoming of twenty over two hundred, just as the qualification of steadfastness is operative here. Its mention was omitted, relying on what has passed and on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah is with the steadfast﴾, for it is a parenthetical concluding interjection confirming the content of what precedes it. What is meant by "being with" is the being with of His help and support. He did not address here the state of the disbelievers regarding abandonment, just as He did not address there the state of the believers, although the basis of overcoming in both cases is the combination of the two matters, namely the help of the believers and the abandonment of the disbelievers, being content with what was mentioned in each context regarding what was omitted in the other context. And what the word (ma'a, "with") indicates of the primacy of what follows it, since they are the ones actually practicing steadfastness, as has passed many times.

﴿Ma kana li-nabiyyin﴾ It is read as (lil-nabiyyi) with the definite article, which refers to a known prophet (al-'ahd). The first reading is more eloquent, because it indicates that what is mentioned is a constant rule (sunnah muttaridah) among the prophets, peace be upon them. That is, it is not proper or fitting for any prophet among the prophets, peace be upon them, ﴿to have captives﴾. The verb is also read with a feminine form, and the word "asra" (captives) is also read as "usara." ﴿Until he has thoroughly subdued (yuthkhina) in the land﴾: that is, he has killed many and gone to extremes in it, until disbelief is humbled and its party is diminished, and Islam is made mighty and its people gain control. The word is from "athkhanahu al-maradu wal-jurhu," meaning when sickness or a wound weighed him down and rendered him unable to move or to rest. Its root meaning is thickness (al-thakhanah), which is coarseness and density. It is also read with the doubled letter for emphasis.

﴿You desire the goods of this world (ʿaraḍa al-dunya)﴾: this is a resumed clause that comes in the form of rebuke, meaning you desire its trifling goods by taking the ransom. It is also read as (yuridu) with the letter ya'. ﴿But God desires the Hereafter﴾: that is, He desires for you the reward of the Hereafter, before which there is no value for this world and what is in it. Or He desires the cause of attaining the Hereafter, which is strengthening His religion and suppressing His enemies. It is also read with the genitive "al-akhirati" (of the Hereafter), by supposing an elided noun, as in the line of poetry:

*Does every man you think a man, and a fire kindling at night a fire?*

﴿And God is Mighty﴾: He overpowers His allies over His enemies. ﴿Wise﴾: He knows what is fitting in every situation and specifies it for it, as He commanded the subduing (al-ithkhan) and forbade taking the ransom when the power belonged to the polytheists, and gave the choice between it and release by His words, Exalted is He: (Then either set them free afterward or take ransom) when the situation changed and victory belonged to the believers.

It is related that the Messenger of God ﷺ was brought seventy captives, among them al-'Abbas and 'Aqil ibn Abi Talib, and he consulted about them. Abu Bakr said: "They are your people and your family; spare them, perhaps God will relent toward them, and take from them a ransom that will strengthen your companions." 'Umar said: "Strike their necks, for they are the leaders of disbelief, and God has made you independent of ransom. Enable 'Ali to take 'Aqil, and Hamzah to take al-'Abbas, and enable me to take so-and-so, a relative of his, and let us strike their necks." The Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed God softens the hearts of men until they become softer than milk, and indeed God hardens the hearts of men until they become harder than stones. Your likeness, O Abu Bakr, is the likeness of Abraham, who said: 'Whoever follows me is indeed of me, and whoever disobeys me, then indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful.' And your likeness, O 'Umar, is the likeness of Noah, who said: 'My Lord, do not leave upon the earth any dweller from among the disbelievers.'" So he gave his companions the choice, and they took the ransom, and then this verse was revealed. 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, entered upon the Messenger of God ﷺ and found him and Abu Bakr weeping. He said: "O Messenger of God, tell me, for if I find weeping I will weep, and if not, I will feign weeping." He said: "I weep over your companions for their taking of the ransom. Their punishment was presented to me, as close as this tree," for a tree that was near to him.

It is also related that he ﷺ said: "Had a punishment come down from the sky, none would have been saved except 'Umar and Sa'd ibn Mu'adh." And he himself was among those who had advised subduing (the enemy).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 68:

﴿Had it not been for a decree from Allah that had already preceded﴾ i.e., had it not been for a ruling from Him, exalted is He, whose establishment had already been recorded in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), namely that He would not punish one who errs in his ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning), or that He would not punish the people of Badr, or a people to whom the prohibition had not been explicitly declared. As for the claim that the ransom they took would become lawful for them, this cannot be counted among the impediments to the touch of punishment, for a later permissibility does not lift the ruling of a prior prohibition, just as a later prohibition, as in the case of wine for example, does not lift the ruling of a prior permissibility. Moreover, this undermines the exaggeration of what was reproached against them concerning the taking of ransom. ﴿Surely there would have touched you﴾ i.e., would have struck you, ﴿for what you took﴾ i.e., because of what you took of ransom, ﴿a great punishment﴾ whose magnitude cannot be measured.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 69:

﴿So eat of what you have taken as booty, being lawful and good﴾. It is narrated that they had refrained from the spoils, and so this was revealed.

Some said: the fa' (fa, "so") is for ordering what follows upon a omitted cause, i.e., "Indeed I have made the spoils lawful to you, so eat of what you have taken as booty." The more apparent view is that it is for conjunction with an implied element required by the context, i.e., "Leave that, and eat of what you have taken as booty." It was also said: "ma" (what) refers to the ransom, for it is among the spoils; but the sequence and context of the noble text reject this.

﴿Halalan﴾ (lawful) is a circumstantial (haal) qualifying the thing taken as booty, or an adjective of the verbal noun, i.e., "eating that is lawful." Its purpose is to encourage eating them. The words of the Exalted, ﴿tayyiban﴾ (good), are an adjective of "halalan," serving to emphasize the encouragement.

﴿And fear Allah﴾, i.e., in opposing His command and prohibition. ﴿Indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, so He will forgive you what has passed from you of seizing the ransom before the permission for it came, and He will show you mercy and turn to you in repentance if you fear Him.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 8, verse 70:**

﴿O Prophet, say to those in your hands﴾, meaning: in your possession, as if your hands were gripping them, ﴿of the captives﴾ (p-37). It is also read as (min al-usara), "of the captives" (a recitational variant, *qira'a*, meaning a different accepted reading of the Qur'anic text). ﴿If Allah knows any good in your hearts﴾, meaning sincerity of faith and soundness of intention, ﴿He will give you better than what was taken from you﴾, meaning the ransom (*fida'*, the payment for the release of captives). It is also read as (akhadha), with the verb in the active voice (*al-bina' lil-fa'il*, a grammatical form in which the verb is built on its doer, here meaning "what He took" rather than "what was taken").

It is related that this verse was revealed concerning al-Abbas. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) charged him with paying the ransom for his two nephews, Aqil ibn Abi Talib and Nawfal ibn al-Harith. He said: "O Muhammad, you have left me to beg from Quraysh for as long as I live." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Then where is the gold that you handed to Umm al-Fadl when you left Mecca? You said to her: 'I do not know what will befall me on this journey; if something happens to me, then it is yours, and for Abdullah, Ubaydullah, and al-Fadl.'" Al-Abbas said: "How could you know that?" He said: "My Lord informed me of it." Al-Abbas said: "I testify that you are truthful, and that there is no god but Allah, and that you are His servant and Messenger. By Allah, no one knew of it except Allah. I gave it to her in the darkness of the night. I was indeed doubtful about your affair, but now that you have informed me of this, there is no doubt."

Al-Abbas said after some time: "Allah has replaced it for me with something better. Now I have twenty slaves, and the least of them trades with twenty thousand. He has given me Zamzam, and I would not wish to have all the wealth of the people of Mecca in exchange for it. And I am awaiting forgiveness from my Lord." This is to be understood in light of His saying, ﴿and He will forgive you, and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. For it is a promise of forgiveness, reinforced by what follows it of the parenthetical concluding clause (*al-i'tiraḍ al-tadhyili*, a phrase inserted into a sentence that closes or summarizes its meaning).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 71:

﴿And if they intend treachery against you﴾, i.e., breaking the pledge they gave you concerning Islam. This statement is directed from God, Exalted is He, to console the Prophet (ﷺ) by way of a promise to him and a warning to them. ﴿Then they had already betrayed God before﴾ by their disbelief and by breaking the covenant taken from every rational being. ﴿So He gave you power over them﴾, i.e., He enabled you to overcome them as you saw on the Day of Badr. So if they return to treachery, know that He will likewise give you power over them. It has been said that the meaning of "treachery" here is withholding what they had guaranteed of ransom, but this is far-fetched.

﴿And God is Knowing﴾, so He knows what is in their intentions and what punishment they deserve. ﴿Wise﴾, He does everything He does in accordance with His perfect wisdom.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 72:

﴿Indeed, those who believed and emigrated﴾ are the muhajirun (the emigrants). They emigrated from their homelands out of love for Allah the Exalted and His Messenger. ﴿And strove with their wealth﴾ by spending it on horses (al-kura') and weapons, and by giving it to the needy. ﴿And their lives﴾ by directly engaging in fighting, plunging into battles, and wading into perils. ﴿In the way of Allah﴾ is connected to "strove," being a restriction on both types of jihad. Perhaps the mention of wealth before lives is because striving with wealth occurs more often and more completely meets the need, since striving with one's person cannot be conceived without striving with wealth.

﴿And those who gave shelter and helped﴾ are the ansar (the helpers). They sheltered the emigrants, lodged them in their own dwellings, gave them their wealth, preferred them over themselves even when they themselves were in need, and helped them against their enemies. ﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to those described by the noble qualities mentioned, and the implication of distance in it is to indicate the elevation of their rank and the remoteness of their station in excellence. It is the subject (mubtada'). The words of Allah the Exalted ﴿some of them﴾ may be a substitute (badal) for it, and His words ﴿are allies of one another﴾ are its predicate; or ﴿some of them﴾ may be a second subject, with ﴿allies of one another﴾ as its predicate, and the whole clause is the predicate of the first subject, meaning: some of them are allies of others in inheritance.

The emigrants and the helpers used to inherit from one another by virtue of emigration and support, to the exclusion of relatives, until this was abrogated by His words ﴿And those of blood relationship have more right﴾ ... the verse. It was also said that it concerns support and backing, but His words ﴿then upon you is the duty of support﴾ after the negation of their being allies refute this.

﴿And those who believed but did not emigrate﴾ like the rest of the believers, ﴿you have no duty of guardianship toward them in any respect﴾, meaning: no share of their inheritance, even if they were among your closest relatives, ﴿until they emigrate﴾. It is read with a kasra on the waw, likening it to a craft or office, like kitabah (writing) and imarah (governorship).

﴿And if they seek your help in religion, then upon you is the duty of support﴾, meaning it is obligatory upon you to support them against the polytheists, ﴿except against a people﴾ among them ﴿between whom and you there is a covenant﴾, a treaty, for it is not permissible to break their covenant by supporting them against those people. ﴿And Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾, so do not oppose His command, lest His punishment befall you.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 73:

﴿And those who disbelieve, some of them are allies of others.﴾ [Meaning:] another among them, in inheritance or in mutual support. This, by its implication (mafhum), indicates the negation of inheritance and mutual support between them and the Muslims, and the necessity of distance and severance, even if they are relatives.

﴿Unless you do it﴾, i.e., what you have been commanded of: maintaining ties among yourselves and taking one another as allies, even in inheritance, and cutting off connections between yourselves and the disbelievers, ﴿there will be a great fitnah (trial, tumult) on earth﴾, i.e., a great strife will occur in it, namely the weakening of faith and the manifestation of disbelief, ﴿and great corruption﴾ in both abodes. It is also read (kathir, "extensive").

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 74:

﴿And those who believed, emigrated, and strove in the way of Allah, and those who gave shelter and helped — these are the true believers.﴾ This is a statement brought forward in praise of them and in testimony to their attainment of the highest rank of faith (al-qidh al-mu'alla, lit. "the top arrow," a metaphor for the foremost place or highest achievement), together with the generous promise in His words, exalted is He: ﴿For them there is forgiveness and a noble provision.﴾ It carries no obligation (tab'a) and no reproach (minna) in it. Therefore there is no repetition, since the purpose of the first statement is to make the bond of mutual support (tawasul) among them obligatory.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 8, verse 75:

﴿And those who believed after [that] and emigrated and strove alongside you — they are of you.﴾ After your emigration (hijrah). ﴿And strove alongside you﴾ in some of your military campaigns (maghazi). ﴿They are of you﴾, i.e., they are of your totality, O emigrants and helpers. They are those who came after them, saying: (Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith). Allah the Exalted joined them to the foremost (al-sabiqun) and made them of them, as a bounty from Him and as an encouragement to faith and emigration. In directing the address to them by way of iltifat (shift of address), there is, in their honour and the elevation of their status, what is not hidden.

﴿And blood relatives (uli al-arham) are closer to one another﴾ than others among them in inheritance (al-tawarruth) from strangers, ﴿in the Book of Allah﴾, i.e., in His judgment, or in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh), or in the Qur'an. It has been cited as evidence for the inheritance of distant kindred (dhawu al-arham). ﴿Indeed Allah is Knowing of all things﴾. Among the things included in this is that inheritance was tied first to religious kinship and last to lineal kinship, which is among the far-reaching wisdoms.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surat al-Anfal and Bara'ah, I will be an intercessor (shafi') for him on the Day of Resurrection and a witness that he is free (bari') from hypocrisy (nifaq), and he will be given ten good deeds for the number of every male hypocrite and female hypocrite, and the Throne and its bearers will seek forgiveness for him during the days of his life." And Allah knows best.
